CONSUMER AND CORPORATE AFFAIRS AND GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS-SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the second report of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations.
I am pleased to table this report entitled Moving the Mail, concerning Canada's postal service in the 1990s. It is the result of extensive study of postal operations by the committee which were begun in October, 1989. Members of all parties worked very hard on this report and we heard submissions and witnesses from across Canada.
Our mandate was to examine the current operations of Canada Post with a view to recommending improvements for the future, improvements in operating efficiencies for Canadians. We had substantial agreement among all three political parties on this report. Out of 39 recommendations we had agreement on approximately
30. The report does include minority reports on those areas where we did not find unanimous agreement.
We found that Canada Post works well today and the more it acts as a private sector corporation the better and more efficient it has proven itself for Canadians. Therefore, we are recommending the eventual privatization of Canada Post. We are recommending a share offering to both Canadians and to employees of Canada Post.
Privatization must be done in an atmosphere of regulation, therefore, we also recommend that Canada Post operations be tightly regulated so that the needs of all Canadians for efficient and effective postal services are maintained.
We also recommend that Canada Post rely on its strengths and put more effort into the sorting and distribution system.

subsubtopic: GOODS AND SERVICES TAX
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the duty to table a petition which has been found correct and certified as to form and content.
The petitioners, who are numerous, would like to humbly submit to this House that the imposition of another tax on Canadians, in particular the goods and services tax of 7 per cent, will be strongly opposed by the majority of Canadians. This tax will cause serious and unfair hardship for low and middle-income Canadians. They say further that the imposition of this tax will create an onerous burden on small business.
They strongly oppose the imposition of the goods and services tax, which in their opinion is an unprecedented tax grab from the pockets of Canadians and will hit us all not only with higher taxes but with higher inflation, higher interest rates and unemployment. The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject the proposed goods and services tax and hope the Senate will do that.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the questionable privilege of rising in the House today to speak to the motion moved by the Deputy Leader of the Govermment in the House of
Commons, and once again, it is a mistake on the part of this government to introduce such a motion.
Madam Speaker, it is the sixth time the government has moved a motion for time allocation in this House, in this Parliament, and it is a dreadful thing because it indicates that the government has lost control of the House and that it does not have the slightest idea how it should introduce bills and motions in this House and deal with public matters that are so very important.
In addition to its sixth motion for time allocation, the government has imposed closure thirteen times during this Parliament, more than any other government in Canada's history. I say that this is the worst government Canada has ever had, because of its failure to deal with the business of this House in a simple and orderly fashion. I say that this government should be deeply ashamed of its failure to accomplish anything important in this House and its failure to deal with government business. Closure thirteen times, time allocation six times and now the seventh time during this Parliament. This is going too far!
The Leader of the Government is not in the House today, but his deputy who is here should be particularly ashamed of the government's decision to table this motion today.

I have spoken many times on the evils of closure in the House, and the way the government treats this Parliament with contempt. I regret that I have to make a similar address today because what we are witnessing in the House is a complete violation of the principles of parliamentary procedure. One only has to look at the rules to see what it is that is contemplated on second reading of a bill.

At the second reading stage, the Standing Orders provide for eight hours of debate after the first three speeches by the minister who introduced the bill, the Official Opposition spokesman and the spokesman for the third party in this House. These three speeches, each of which may last forty minutes, are not included in the eight hours of debate. Subsequently, eight hours of debate are provided: twenty minutes for each speech, plus ten minutes for questions and comments. We now have a situation where there have been practically no bills on which the government has allowed eight hours of debate during this Parliament. Perhaps on the abortion bill, but otherwise, practically no bills had eight hours of debate before closure or time allocation was imposed.
April 24, 1990

After those eight hours, what do the Standing Orders say? Ten minutes for each speech, and we have not had a single ten-minute speech on this bill. We have had only two hours and twenty-one minutes out of the eight hours provided by the Standing Orders for each bill considered by the House. And before those two hours and twenty-one minutes were up, the government gave notice of this motion for time allocation.
[English)
It is a shocking outrage that the government would proceed in this fashion. It is unable to come to negotiate any arrangement with respect to public business. It does not seem interested in negotiations and is interested only in allowing the bill through.
The approach of the government to this House is: "We don't want to hear your debate on this bill. We just want to know when you're gonna pass it. It is adopted as is. Pass it as is and, if you don't want to pass it, then we'll just impose closure and get it through anyway." There is no desire to listen to the opposition.
I was elected to represent Canadians in the House, as was every member of the opposition. We have a right and a duty to discuss bills in the House and to point out their shortcomings and their failures to the government. Yet, the government's expectation is that we will do that in three or four speeches, and then allow the thing through. That is the expectation.
I can think back to Parliaments in years past when I followed the proceedings of the House-not as a member-either from them galleries or by reading the debates. Many debates on many bills went on for a week or two weeks at a time. We have not had the luxury of any such debate in this Parliament. What is the urgency? There is no urgency. The government lets us go on extended breaks from sitting here. When we come back, it says: "We want this bill through in two days, one day or three days." Three days is usually the maximum.

speechtext: They're nervous about defections.

They are nervous about defections, as the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood points out. The government has had two defections already and I hear there is going to be a flood of them coming up. Rats off a sinking ship!
Aside from that, they have clearly had to debate these bills for so long in cabinet that they are bored with the debate. They say: "We've heard it all now. We don't need to listen to members of the Opposition on this bill." Their cabinet obviously is badly divided on these issues. They cannot make up their minds. They finally do long after the bill should have been introduced. They come waltzing along to the House, drop the bill onto the table, and say: "Pass it now."
That is the attitude of the government House leader. It is a bad attitude. I hope the new deputy government House leader will avoid that attitude, will chastize his boss, and try to get it changed. It is the wrong approach to the operations of a parliamentary democracy.
This Parliament exists to debate these bills, to point out their shortcomings, and to give the people of Canada who are opposed to some of these measures the opportunity to express their opposition and disapproval.
The government feels, probably because the bills are so dreadful, that, rather than listen to the people, it is simply going to cut off debate at every opportunity. We have had it cut off, as I have indicated, so many times. There have been 20 times now in this Parliament by either closure or time allocation. It is too many. It has gone on too long, and this debate has not gone on long

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
enough. Yet, here we have the government trying to silence the people of Canada.
I challenge any one of the ministers who was elected to serve in the House to stand on his feet to participate in the debate on this bill and allow the debate to go for more than one more day as proposed by the deputy government House leader. They, too, were elected by their constituents.
The people of Kingston and the Islands had enough of this government in the last election campaign in 1988. They wanted representation in this House that was effective, that would be a voice to speak up for their rights that were being violated by this government by the passage of the kind of motion that is being introduced here today. They did not expect to have a member of Parliament whose views would be stifled by continuous application of closure and time allocation such as has gone on in this House 20 times already in this Parliament, and we have not yet sat two years.
Never before has a Canadian Parliament been treated to this kind of abuse. It constitutes an abuse of the rights of all parliamentarians and a contempt of this House of the worst kind. The Deputy House Leader should have the rummel gumption to stand up and withdraw this motion at once and apologize to the House for having introduced it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, to echo my colleague's last words, I wonder if the Deputy House Leader would not want to resign from his position, because I cannot imagine that the Deputy House Leader is serious when he says that we have had enough time for debate on Bill C-69. After all, Madam Speaker, this is a bill that is going cap federal government support for post-secondary education, for health and hospital care and for social services and social assistance in the provinces. In other words, this bill goes against the very grain of what a Canadian and what Canada is all about. Yet the government says we have had enough debate.
Madam Speaker, we have only started the debate. Once again, we have only had less than three hours of discussion on this most important piece of budget legislation that we are going to debate in the next number of months and after two hours and 20 minutes of debate the government says: "We have had enough, we do not want
to hear any more dissent, we do not want to hear any more opposition voices. We do not want to be reminded of what it is we are doing; we do not want the people of Canada to understand what the government is doing".
This comes at a very interesting time. In another part of the world, in some of the communist countries in eastern Europe, the governments are opening up their Parliaments; they are saying that they are prepared to listen to a dissenting voice. They are prepared to recognize that the opposition has a role. They are prepared to listen to voices that criticize what the government of the day is doing.
That is going on in eastern Europe, and the world rejoices at that. Yet in our own country, with the Progressive Conservative government, time after time after time the government says it is not going to permit those people who were elected by the people of Canada to express their views in the House of Commons that opportunity.
Look at the benches today. The benches on the opposition side are filled today. I suspect that all of us on the opposition side want to speak out against the government's cuts to post-secondary education and to health care. Yet the government says it is not going to permit the House of Commons to function as the House of Commons is supposed to function. It is not going to permit members of the opposition to express their views on this legislation. It is not going to permit the democratic system to work in the country.

Madam Speaker, that is the usual inane comment that we would expect from that member. I am not even going to refer to what is sitting across on the government side and be caught in that same nonsense. But you will see, Madam Speaker, that he will not participate in this debate because he is embarrassed and the best criticism he can make is to rise in his place and make a nonsense comment about attendance in the House of Commons when it is his government that is forcing the goods and services tax down the throats of every Canadian against their will.
April 24, 1990

Eighty per cent of Canadians say that they oppose this legislation; 80 per cent say: "Do not proceed". Yet this government says it is the big brother government, it is hiring thousands of tax collectors. The government says that it knows what is best for Canadians, it does not listen to any alternatives. It is the big brother of the system now; it has the majority; it is arrogant. It can do anything it wants to the people of Canada, including jamming this tax down their throats.
That is the kind of government we have-an arrogant government, a government that is undemocratic, a government that has contempt for the House of Commons, a government that has no respect for the parliamentary traditions of this country, because if it had it would permit debate on one of the most important pieces of budget legislation before the House.
But it does not and the point I was making is that, as you can see, there are opposition members here who were elected to represent their constituencies. They were elected to speak out on legislation that is before this House and this government will not allow the opposition to do that. This government will not allow the people of Canada to be heard.
That is why I say that there is the sound of jackboots in this building at the moment. You can hear jackboots crashing across on the government benches as their dictatorial, totalitarian ways are perpetuated time after time.
I ask my friends opposite whether they can remember a government in the history of Canada that has used closure so many times to muzzle debate in the House of Commons. There has never been a government that has used the heavy hand of muzzling Parliament time and time and time again. As a matter of fact, just in this short Parliament it has been used 13 times on legislation on which the government has refused to allow proper debate.
You know as well as I, Madam Speaker, that we only allow eight hours of full debate and after that we get into 10 minute speeches by members. That curtails debate after two or three days normally. After only one hour of debate the government gave notice that it has had enough. I say that that is not the democratic tradition that people in this country have fought to uphold for generations. This government has said to the people of Canada: "We have the majority now and we are going to
Government Orders
do whatever we want, including making the Parliament of Canada irrelevant".
I still cannot believe that my hon. friends sitting across the way are so determined to jam this goods and services tax down the throat of every Canadian because they actually support it, and yet it seems that they do because they vote time and time again in support of that legislation.
We have a job to do, and our constituents expect us to do that job. The job of representatives of the opposition parties is to offer criticism to the government's legislation when it is brought forward. If it is good legislation, we support it. We have, on many occasions, with very little debate and on occasion with no debate, simply passed good legislation.
But when we see a bill like Bill C-69 through which the government is going to essentially abandon the support we in this country have known for post-secondary education, naturally a number of us want to speak against that particular initiative. After all, the young people in this country are the lifeblood of the country. They are the most important resource we have in Canada. Our young people are pursuing post-secondary education so that they can play their rightful roles in an information-based economy of the 1990s and beyond. Yet this government says, presumably, that it does not believe in young people. It does not believe in funding post-secondary education. It does not believe in doing what virtually every other western industrialized nation is doing, that is investing in our most important resource which is the young people of our country.
The government is going to cap support for post-secondary education. Can you imagine anything more regressive, more thoughtless than that? If the people of Canada knew what the government is doing, if they understood that this government is not going to continue funding the hospitals of Canada, is not going to continue supporting health care and medicare in this country as we have known it in the past, is not going to support our universities, vocational schools, technical schools and colleges as it has done in the past, the people of Canada would be even more cynical of the role the government is playing.
To stave off this opposition the government is going to try to keep the people of Canada from knowing what it is doing. The best way it can do that is to silence the House of Commons, to silence the opposition benches from exposing what this government is attempting to do in these critical areas of health care and post-secondary

April 24, 1990

education. The government has announced now that it is going to close off debate, that it is not going to allow members of the opposition, or perhaps even members of the government, to express their views.
I submit that that is undemocratic, that it goes against the very parliamentary traditions that we have upheld and felt so strongly about in our country for generations, and that it adds to the dislike of the people of Canada for this government. How can you, Madam Speaker, respect a government that is anti-democratic? How can you respect a government that is totalitarian in its approach to the House of Commons? How can you respect a government that is anti-democratic day after day by muzzling the members of the House of Commons?
The fact that only 16 per cent of the people of Canada now reluctantly support this government-and that number is probably dropping-is no surprise.
In closing, I suggest that if this government continues to be so anti-Parliament in its process, to be so antiHouse of Commons, to be so anti-democratic, not only will it lose the 16 per cent of the support of the people of Canada, it will erode even further and this government deserves the erosion of that support.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext:
Thke a look at the democratic institutions in this world and you will find that we are the longest winded legislature in the democratic free world. We sit more days, talking longer. There have only been two debates since 1950, at second reading, that have gone longer than two days in the British House of Commons. Debate went six days when they entered into the European Economic Community and three days when they got rid of the Greater London Council.
I had the opportunity of sitting on the opposition side for 12 years. I know how it used to be. The idea is to talk, talk, talk, to try to force the government to bring in closure or time allocation. I know it is a tactic which is used.
I really think that we in the House of Commons are on the edge of talking ourselves into irrelevancy. I think we should sit down and modernize what we are doing in this place. We should come in tune with the times. The member for Kingston and the Islands was talking of a week or two weeks for debate at second reading stage, yet they go for a maximum of two days in England on second reading.
There is lots of time. We are going to have another six hours of debate on this. There is going to be a chance for more discussion.
We really have to look at the fundamental way in which we run this place. Instead of always just opposing, getting counteracting ideas from the government side and then comments from the opposition, I think we should sit down and fundamentally look at how we run this place.
For example, I know the stall tactics of putting up petitions. In England every petition gets filed with the Clerk. They respond to them. We can file with the Clerk here. We do not have to stand up and spend hours of House of Commons time reading them. Nobody ever watches it on TV and nobody reports them in the paper. They are reported in the Order Paper when they are
April 24, 1990

filed so you get as much printed press as you do when you stand up and talk about them.
We can make some observations of how other Parliaments run their affairs. Instead of becoming irrelevant and wasting time, I think we should try and organize ourselves. Perhaps on an all-party basis the House Leaders would want to sit down to organize ourselves in a better way, instead of talking about such ridiculous stuff as jackboots.
You have to admit, when you get that sort of trash introduced as a speech in the House of Commons you have to question why we are standing here taking up time, why we are spending the money, why we are being so foolish.
So let us become a little more sensible and more realistic in the modern day. Let us use Parliament to debate matters and move on. We do not have to drag them out for a week or two weeks at a time. We have to move them along. I do not think we have to hear such trash as having two weeks debate on this, that and the other thing, or that it is a place of jackboots.
Closure and time allocation has been around for a long time. You can count the number of times the Liberals used it in the last Parliament before they turned the reins over to the Conservatives. They used it many times. We used it many times in the last Parliament. The pressures of the times are going to be realized. Nobody even comments on it any more in the press because it is used so regularly and they know it has to be, otherwise the opposition will just hold things up.
We saw what the NDP did on the goods and services tax. The very party which agreed with the goods and services tax in 1987 is now trying to talk it out at committee and in the House of Commons, through all kinds of procedural tactics, rather than getting on with it.
The government has the right to propose things. The House of Commons should dispose of things. The opposition may wish to oppose on certain occasions, it may wish to agree on certain occasions. If we oppose on all occasions and try to hold up the disposition of things for one week, two weeks, or three weeks, we become irrelevant here. I think we should look at the fundamen-
Govemment Orders
tals of the system, otherwise it is going to become a jackboot and irrelevant place.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to express my disappointment at the cutting off of debate and the use of time allocation on a very important topic for the people of my region and the people of my city.
I cannot believe that in the alleged interests of modernizing this place, we as members of Parliament should choose our topics for debate and decide the business of this Chamber on the basis of whether the press gallery is empty or full. Even to suggest that is to denigrate the work that is done here and done ably by members on both sides of the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext: Not always.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext:
Definitely not always, and I am glad the member recognizes that. However, the question of time allocation on this particular bill is one that cannot be allowed to go by without strong protest from elected members of Parliament.
What we have here is time allocation on cuts to post-secondary education. What we have here is time allocation on cuts to health care. What we have here is time allocation on capping the Canada Assistance Plan.
In my region in the Atlantic people depend very much on funding such as this to maintain some sort of level playing field with the rest of the country. The people in the Atlantic region, the strongest supporters of post-secondary education in this country, see, along with all of the other things that have been thrown at them by this government in the past five years, the almost total erosion of federal funding for absolutely necessary services.
Are their elected representatives, the majority of whom sit on the opposition side of the House, being given a fair amount of time to put forward their views? No, they are not. The government has used its garotte and time allocation has been brought in for the twentieth time in the young life of this particular session.
When the universities in Atlantic Canada see that they can no longer offer the number of programs that they offered before these cuts were made, when those same universities see that they cannot pay their faculty and their staff according to the levels that are paid in the rest

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
of the country, they are going to remember that their elected representatives were cut off in debate and not permitted to put forward the views of the people of the Atlantic region.
When health care cutbacks seriously affect the quality of life of Atlantic Canadians, Atlantic Canadians are going to remember that this was the twentieth time in a Parliament that commenced sitting in December, 1988, that this government said that it does not matter what the opposition thinks, it does not matter what the people represented by opposition members want to say and want to have said on their behalf, all that matters is that this bill gets tabled and gets passed as fast as humanly possible.
This chamber is an historic and almost mystical place for those of us fortunate enough to come here to represent our fellow Canadians. If we do not give this chamber and all its works the respect and time due to it, then we create in those people whom we represent from the Atlantic to the Pacific a sense that we are useless, that we are not here for any purpose. I do not believe that, you do not believe that, Madam Speaker, and neither, I believe, do the members opposite believe that.
But perception in politics, perception in government, means a whole lot more a great deal of the time than actuality. To use this Draconian measure 20 times is something that Canadians are not going to put up with.
I realize that the government has a fear of having a long drawn out debate on this because it is unfair. I realize that the government will do anything to avoid long discussions on the fact that it is cutting back on programs that mean survival to institutions and to health care programs, to child care programs and to various other social institutions in this country without which the lives of individual Canadians are going to be bleaker and more difficult with a loss of hope and, sadly, a loss of interest in how this country works.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext: And service.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext:
And yes, service as well, absolutely.
I suppose, after listening to my learned colleague from Kingston and the Islands, my distress and upset at what this government is doing in this particular case is tempered, again sadly, with a sense of cynicism that it
does not matter what you do, whether it is good or bad, as long as you do it quickly so people will forget.
So we will do these things that are counter-productive for Canadians, we will do these things that are going to close hospital beds all over Atlantic Canada, that are going to shut down university classrooms all over Atlantic Canada, that are going to cut out of much needed day care spaces in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. We are going to cut back so that the university education, of which Canadians have long been so rightly proud from coast to coast, is no longer an asset that Canadians can put on the international market and say: "Here we are. We can hold up our educational backgrounds and our training with anyone", so that the government can sweep yet another massive whiplash attack on its citizens under the rug of parliamentary procedure.
For 20 years I have watched and studied the Canadian political system, going right back to the great pipeline debate of the 1950s when closure was introduced by a Liberal government, to its great detriment. Canadian citizens talk veiy little about the procedures that we go through in this House. Frequently they have neither the time nor the inclination to watch what we do in this House. But closure is something that Canadians do understand. They do understand the stifling of debate and they do understand what it means when their duly elected representatives are precluded by the government from doing the job that they were elected to do. Certainly, Madam Speaker, they do understand that when these things are said by members of the government, and when opposition members are told that the importance of their work here in this Chamber can only be gauged by whether or not it makes the national news, the national newspapers or the early morning radio, then I think Canadians have a right to stand together and cry "halt".
This bill that is being cut off from debate deals a blow to the citizens of my region and to the citizens of all the regions of Canada. It is wrong that the time for full debate and the time for full discussion of what Canadians want from their federal government should be shoved into some small comer of the parliamentary calendar and left again to be swept away because the government feels, in its bizarre and ultimate wisdom, that it knows what is best for Canadians, and that what is
April 24, 1990

best for Canadians is not having elected members of Parliament stand and oppose, as they are constitutionally elected to do.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to also speak against the time allocation motion on Bill C-69. I am disappointed that once again this government is thwarting the rights of the representatives of the people of Canada to be heard on an important issue.
Since I have been elected, time and again we have seen from this government time allocation motions, closure motions, the stifling of debate in the House of Commons. The attitude of this government appears to be to not bother with the democratic process, to not listen to the ordinary folks of Canada. We have even seen this government drag off Parliament Hill protesters who were peacefully protesting against this government's actions.
The Tories do not want to hear what the people of Canada, the Official Opposition, or the New Democratic Party has to say about Bill C-69. They have made that very clear.
Clause 2 of Bill C-69 limits spending under the Canada Assistance Plan to only 5 per cent for British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. This will affect social assistance, child care and shelters for battered women. That is the mechanism for funding those programs in this country between the provinces and the federal government.
Provinces and territories other than British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario are exempt from this capping for the time being. That does not mean that in the next round the government will not attack their social programs, their child care and their shelters for battered women as well.
The government is dismantling social programs. The government promised child care before two elections and then scrapped the plans for a child care program immediately after the elections. The government completely cut core funding to women's centres so that women's centres that provided referrals to shelters for battered women are closing. Already 10 centres have closed in British Columbia. Now the government is going even one step further and attacking the shelters them-
Government Orders
selves, the child care programs that were already in place and the poor of those three provinces.
As my colleague, the member for Mission-Coquitlam, has already said, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia may be better off in this nation, but the poor in those three provinces are just as poor as the poor citizens in any other province. Approximately 46 per cent of all persons receiving assistance under CAP live in those three provinces.
The finance minister is predicting higher unemployment. At the same time his government is hacking at the unemployment insurance program. There will be nothing left for these people to live on but social assistance. Now the Tories are trying to restrict that too.
Some analysts say that the 5 per cent growth limit will only just cover inflation. It will not be anywhere near adequate enough to cover the increased need that has been created by Tory economic mismanagement.
What will it be next? The Tories have already attacked pensions. They have already attacked family allowance programs. What is left for this government to attack?
There is already a child care crisis in this country. In my province of British Columbia there are only 20,000 licensed spaces for the 300,000 children requiring care. British Columbia is one of the provinces that has been slapped with a spending limit on child care.
Violence against women in our society is a serious and an urgent problem. It is something we hear members on the government side mouth platitudes about, but what women really need is action to address this problem.
One in every two shelters for battered women must turn women and their children away because they lack space to house them. That is how it is right now. The Tories have chosen at this time to slap a spending limit on shelters for battered women in those three provinces. It is shameful.
In my province of British Columbia, the provincial government-the cousins of the Conservative government, the Social Credit Party-have already choked the poor. There are two food banks in operation in my constituency. Those food banks have been in operation for many years now. They have become institutionalized in British Columbia. This is not the time-nor is there

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
any time-for the federal government to abdicate its responsibility toward Canadians.
In 1981, a parliamentary task force stated that the federal government has "a constitutional responsibility for programs of income redistribution, including social assistance programs paying money to Canadians anywhere in Canada".
This government has ignored the requirement in the Canada Assistance Plan to give the provinces one year's notice of any change in CAP funding. The federal government is currently being challenged in the courts by British Columbia as to its illegal and unethical practices concerning CAP.
The Canada Assistance Plan was first introduced in the 1960s as one of five measures to reduce poverty in Canada. Canadians know now-if they did not know before-that the Tories really only care about their rich friends, the friends and the insiders of this government. It proves it to us every day. It proved that it does not have an inkling of feeling, respect or of concern for lower and middle-income Canadians.
We have heard members on the government side talk about the savings from cutting the CAP. Who is saving? If the federal government saves, provincial governments have to spend more. It all comes out of the same taxpayer's pocket. It is ordinary Canadians who pay the bills in this country. There is absolutely no savings for the Canadian taxpayer. They only see their taxes going one way-and that is up. They pay more and more taxes and receive fewer and fewer services from this government. There is really only increased hardship for those at the lower end of the economic spectrum.
People who need jobs and food, children without anyone to care for them, battered women-these are the people who are paying for this federal government's imaginary savings.
This government is behaving in a disgusting way. We have the right to speak out. That is the democratic process. We have the right to speak out about what the Tories are doing to our country. We have the right to say that we have had enough of this government's economic mismanagement.
We want care for our children. Women want somewhere to turn to when they are battered. They do not
want to find the doors of women's centres locked. They do not want to go to a shelter when they have been abused and battered and find there is no space for them or for their children.
We want our children to have food to eat. Canadians do not want to line up at food banks, to be seen standing at the door of a charitable institution. They want a decent standard of care for themselves and for their children. They want decent jobs. They want to have a secure future for themselves and their families.
That is what Canada is about. Canada is about free speech, about a caring and a compassionate society. It is about good social programs and security for all its people. That is what this government is trying so hard to destroy.
We want the opportunity to express fully our opposition to this bill. I urge all members of the House not to support the time allocation motion on this important bill and, further, to vote down this unethical bill, Bill C-69.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are witnessing today another sad event in the history of Parliament. This is the first time that a government has had to give notice of two measures to stifle debate, to apply the guillotine to parliamentary proceedings. To justify its ends any means is now to be used.
Indeed, a sign of a desperate government that does not know how to administer the House of Commons or how to manage the time of the House of Commons is when it has to throw the book at the opposition, as it did yesterday, and give notice that on the one hand it might use closure, but on the other it might use time allocation.
Those are the two measures at the government's disposal to cut off debate. This bill is a very important measure put forward to cut expenditures of the federal government in many important fields of Canadian systems and programs under the EPF dealing with health care and education. EPF is the program under which the government funds post-secondary education, health care and some of the Canada Assistance Programs.
It has been said before in this House, and I think it is worth repeating, that this is the twentieth time the government has moved such a motion in this Parliament. It is the thirty-fifth time that the Tory government has used either closure or time allocation since it took power
April 24, 1990

in 1984. That does not say much for its capacity to administer the House.
However, it says much about the jackboot approach to the opposition in trying to prevent democratic debate on important matters. It says much about not giving the opposition a chance to explain to Canadians what is in the legislation. The government surely does not explain to Canadians what it is doing. That is possibly why today it is the least popular party in the history of this country. Some 15 per cent of Canadians, at best-according to the results of the latest Gallup poll-support the Tories.
In my view, it is a sign of a government in trouble, a government which is desperately trying to shut off debate to prevent Canadians from hearing the truth about its legislative programs. What does it do? It imposes the guillotine. It cuts off debate after less than two hours and fifteen minutes on a bill that is very important to Canadians which deals with programs to which we in Canada attach great importance. I am talking about programs which fund post-secondary education and health care-one of the best programs in the world-and the Canada Assistance Plan which has been capped in certain provinces.
It is as though the poor in Ontario, my province, were any different from the poor anywhere else in this country. The poor in Ottawa-Vanier are just as much in need of attention as any other poor people in this country. This Tory government is saying to the people of my riding of Ottawa-Vanier: "If you are poor, we are sorry, but you are going to have to submit yourselves to a system which is absolutely unable to respond with care, understanding and generosity".
I cannot understand why this government would use at this stage-as I said before, after less than two hours and fifteen minutes of debate-time allocation, a form of closure, on a bill of such great importance to Canadians. I cannot understand why it would allow one additional day of debate, which could possibly be tomorrow, a Wednesday, which is a very short day, giving us less than the normal eight hours allowed on second reading of a bill before we proceed to the 10-minute speeches. The 10-minute speeches are a way of getting more members of Parliament involved in debate. In that way we can hear

from all the regions of this country, from all the people duly elected in this House.
A government which has by all accounts fewer friends than supporters than any party has ever had in the history of this country is indeed in trouble. -because, Madam Speaker, this government measure, Bill C-69, is aimed at reducing transfer payments to the provinces for higher education, slashing health care programs, and capping funds paid to Ontario, my province, Alberta and British Columbia under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Since 1986, Madam Speaker, this is the third time the government has been gunning for Established Programs Financing. I have it here: total EPF cut-backs between 1986-87 and 1994-95 will amount to the astronomical sum of $31.1 billion, that is reductions of $22.2 billion which should have been earmarked for healh care, and $8.9 billion for higher education. Should the provinces decide not to raise their taxes they will have to force hospitals to close a number of beds or perform fewer surgical operations to make up for these cut-backs, or again require students to pay higher tuition fees, work in overcrowded lecture halls and probably abandon their studies because they will be unable to afford tuition fees for courses for which they would otherwise be entitled to register. And yet it was on March 24, 1982 that the same Minister of Finance who is sponsoring this measure and first presented it to Parliament in his budget said, and I

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
quote: "Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems outside of that arena."
Madam Speaker, that is exactly what he is doing now. He has started a terrible debate between the provinces and the federal government. He is putting the future of our young people and the health of Canadians at risk. He is abdicating the role of the federal government, which is to redistribute, to help and to give each province the funds it needs, so that we can have a universal, non-profit health-care system open to all Canadians. I must say that this government totally abdicates its responsibilities when it withdraws from shared-cost programs, when it decides to drop these programs and tell the provinces it is their constitutional responsibility and to get on with it! Madam Speaker, this attitude is very bad for our country. It is an attitude that should be condemned. And I again condemn the government for having introduced time allocation today, a measure that will prevent us, the Official Opposition, from informing Canadians of the serious and negative impact this legislation will have on the future of our country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-ALLOCATION OF TIME FOR THE CONSIDERATION AT SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL-69
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member mentioned abdication, and I say it is the Liberal Party and the NDP who are doing the abdicating.

What are they abdicating? Any sense of responsibility for the affairs of this nation and for the people of this nation. They do it consistently time after time in the Chamber. They did it consistently year after year as a
government with the aid and support of the New Democratic Party.
I remember being a brand new member in the House. I had the honour, on behalf of our party, to be the second speaker in a budget debate. The NDP moved a motion to get rid of that budget. The Liberals supported it. We were in a minority situation. The budget was defeated and we were gone.
What did they defeat? They defeated a budget that was acclaimed subsequently by analysts to be the fairest budget to the poor people of the nation in the decade of the seventies. Then they presume to stand in the Chamber again today and say they are standing up on behalf of ordinary Canadians from the provinces and regions.
The Liberal Party of Canada left us an absolute mess in the financial sense. We have stood up in the Chamber to present a simple piece of legislation that deals with the control of public expenditures, and that says this nation has gone on for far too long spending and borrowing. We have reached a point where 35 cents out of a revenue dollar simply pays interest on the public debt. Yet, members opposite stand up in the Chamber time after time and say: "That is not bad enough, let's make it worse. Let's spend, spend, spend. Don't raise taxes. Don't get any revenue. Just borrow, borrow, borrow."
Sooner or later $1 out of every $1 in revenue is going to have to pay the interest on the public debt. There will not be a penny for policing, there will not be a penny for the environment, and there will not be a penny for the senior citizens of the country, if we follow the advice which flows from across the Chamber to this side. The opposition says: "Don't cut your expenditures. Expand your expenditures. Don't raise revenue. Borrow, borrow, borrow". That is the mentality that sits on the other side of the Chamber.
They then have the gall to stand up in the Chamber to say that we are cutting off debate. That is the bunch- and I include both parties on the other side of the Chamber-which has refused time after time offers to extend debate in the Chamber, to meet later in the evening, to meet until midnight, or to meet on weekends to discuss a measure for an entire weekend. They say: "No, no, no, we want the House to shut down at the scheduled time. We want days and days of debate at second reading. This would give us the time to put our
April 24, 1990

prejudgments on the table. We could put our philosophy on the table. But we would make no advancement on the passage of legislation which is designed to help the people of the nation."
We should take a lesson from Parliaments with, perhaps, more history than we have yet to offer-Parliaments that have been around for hundreds of years.
In those Parliaments, the normal time of debate at second reading is between one and two hours. Why? Because they have learned through experience that, when a bill passes out of the House at second reading and into committee, they can tap the expertise which exists in a nation to look at whether or not the fine print is right for the nation. The examination of a piece of legislation has to be done with the help of people knowledgeable in the field, people with more knowledge than we as individual members of Parliament in most cases bring with us to the Chamber.
We get the help of witnesses in committee to look at the fine print. We have an opportunity to study a piece of legislation for days, weeks, or months, depending on its complexity, its importance, and the willingness of Canadians who have the knowledge base to assist us in the fine-tuning of that piece of legislation.
After that, the legislation should come back to the Chamber where it should move rather quickly through report stage and third reading. If there are amendments members want to propose at report stage, then they should be considered. Short speeches should be made about them. The House is either persuaded or not. We should then vote on them, and they should be disposed of.
The entire process for second reading, report stage and third reading, in terms of actual time in the Chamber, should be no more than a day in almost every case, or a day and a half in the unusual case. Yet what do we find on this particular piece of legislation? Even after we pass the motion for time allocation today, it will have taken three days simply for second reading stage in the Chamber. It will have cost a minimum of $3 million of public time and expense. That is $3 million to listen to the kind of drivel that people watching television are
Government Orders
hearing in the Chamber today. That is only through second reading.
After second reading, it has to go through committee and then comes back to report and for third reading stage. How many more days will the jokers on the other side of the Chamber want to spend on it? How many more millions of dollars of taxpayers' funds will they want to spend standing in the Chamber spewing rhetoric that is not based on reality? We should not be voting on time allocation today, we should be voting on the bill.
It is very, very simple. Does the House believe that the time has come to cut public expenditures? Or, does the House believe that we should continue to expand public expenditures?
The only thing at issue here today is whether or not there is a single, responsible individual on the other side of this Chamber-even one member of the opposition- who is not under their Whip's control and who has the courage to stand up in this Chamber and vote for this measure. Some of them come from backgrounds from which they know that you cannot continue to expand public expenditures and to borrow money without creating massive inflation, massive unemployment, and massive problems for the senior citizens and others in the country.
That is the prescription that was in place, basically, from 1972 through until 1984, which those two parties followed. Their philosophy was: "Spend, spend, spend. Don't raise money. Borrow, borrow, borrow."
What did that philosophy lead to? It led to the worst unemployment rates this country has ever seen. It led to interest rates of up to 24 per cent and inflation rates that were absolutely killing for people on fixed incomes, the seniors of this country. It created enormous problems of spousal battering resulting from family tensions and monetary tensions. Divorce rates were rocketing out of sight because of the same kinds of tensions. It was an absolute disaster for the country.
There were twelve years of gradually increasing disaster. Many of us in the Chamber watched it. Those of us who were not in the Chamber then were watching it from outside. Now, they want to go back to it. They want to stall the Chamber from taking the sensible steps which need to be taken.

April 24, 1990

Looking down the hall to the other place, we see the legislation that is piling up. For example, there is a piece of legislation related to unemployment insurance that would enable us to provide training to Canadians. They need that training to be able to hold jobs, to make our industries more productive, and to make our economy better and our standard of living higher. Members opposite stalled it here for months and months, and then an unelected place down the hall stalls it for months and months. They then stand up here and say that we, on this side, are against democracy.
As you know, Madam Speaker, there was an election and we won it. We are responsible for our programs, but now they are trying to make us responsible for their obstinance, their obstructionism, and their waste of dollars in this Chamber. That is what they would like us to be responsible for. I say Canadians are too wise.
Canadians know that when they do not have the money in their family budgets they have to cut. Canadians know that it is the job of this Chamber, if it is going to act responsibly, to move quickly on those measures required to cut public expenditures and to get expenditures under control in the best interest of Canadians from one coast of the country to the other and from north to south. All Canadians will benefit from the passage of this legislation, an initiative whose time has come.
We have the obligation to get on with it, and to get on with it today as quickly as possible, and to get over this silly nonsense of obstructing things that are indeed in the national interest.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a few words to say concerning this particular motion before the House, and a few words concerning the address just given by the hon. member opposite.
There are two primary functions of this Chamber. One function is legislative. The other function is accountability of the Government of Canada to the people of Canada. Simply to say that there is only one function for a Parliament is to overlook perhaps the main function of legislatures throughout the world which have established their procedure under what we call the British parliamentary system.
The hon. member who just spoke went into some detail in putting forward the argument that other legislatures in other countries under the British parliamentary system have rules that mean, for example, that a motion must come to an end at the end of the sitting day. Instead of having this particular piece of legislation before the House for three days, as the hon. member said, it would go through in one day and then to a committee of the House. After careful examination in committee where the real work is done, it would then come back to the House.
However, what the hon. member is overlooking, of course, is that, although that may be one difference between the Parliament of Canada and the Parliament of Great Britain or Australia, there are other differences that make up for the loss of accountability that one finds in time limitation measures enshrined in the parliamentary rules of those legislatures. Most of the Parliaments that have built into their rules a time factor that a motion comes to an end at the end of the sitting day also have committees that originate their own terms of reference. In other words, the real accountability and the action in those Parliaments are in the committees. They are not in the Parliaments themselves.
You say that the legislature is separate from the Parliament. Even in Question Period notice is given of a question, but the committees originate their own terms of reference. They decide what they will do. That is where the accountability function has been established for those legislatures.
It is unfortunate that over the years the Parliament of Canada has lost that aspect of accountability. That is that the executive would be accountable to the people through the Parliament of Canada. That is the primary function of the Parliament of Canada. We have evolved our system to the point where if you examine the rules correctly, you find that no minister has to answer a question. If you examine the precedents of the Canadian parliamentary system, you find that no minister is held accountable for actions of his department or his officials. It is a far ciy from Erskine May and Beauchesne to what we have today. To remove the accountability factor and to keep bringing in time allocation or closure on legislation removes from the Parliament of Canada its most important function.
April 24, 1990

The hon. member mentioned that three days of debate was long enough for second reading of this particular piece of legislation. I have to question that. The legislation that he was referring to puts a cap on and limits spending by the federal treasurer. I will use the transfers to the provinces for health and post-secondary education as an example. Once upon a time, Madam Speaker, we had what we called the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Care Act under which the Parliament of Canada had to pay to the provinces certain sums of money for the operations of hospitals. That changed a few years ago to block funding. The provinces do not necessarily have to spend that money on those particular operations but they certainly cannot afford in this day and age to have the Government of Canada saying: "Look, for the purposes of running hospitals and running your health care scheme in your province and in running your post-secondary institutions the Government of Canada is going to limit expenditures." It is not only that but it is even more serious when you consider what is actually taking place in those two areas. There were two areas that you would never touch if you had a choice and if you had a certain amount of money in the government treasury. The two areas that you should never touch should be health and post-secondary education. If there is an area that should be beyond the axe, it should be hospitals and health care.
In this day and age we have many new machines and inventions to be purchased and operated by our hospitals. Certain provinces in our nations do not have certain machines for health care and other provinces do have machines for health care. In certain provinces there are patients waiting in the corridors to receive medical treatment there instead of in hospital rooms. People wait in line for days and weeks and months for bypass surgery. When you have all of those things taking place, certainly the one area you would not dare touch-you would not think about it, you would not contemplate it and you would not dream about it-is health care. You would not touch that at all if you knew the facts and realized how important our hospitals are and how important our health care system is. That is what the Government of Canada has done. So when the hon. member says "Well, you know, it is going to take three days for second reading on this bill", the Canadian public is saying it should take three years.

The Parliament of Canada is supposed to hold the Government of Canada accountable for the people of Canada. That is the function of this Parliament. It is not to simply legislate. If that is the sole function of Parliament then let us get rid of the opposition parties totally. Let us have only one system brought in whereby the government will only introduce the legislation and no one will say anything about it at all.

I am sure that the Tories do not want this information fully before the public. How can a member of the House of Commons possibly desire that end result? It is simple mathematics. If your revenues are not equal to your expenditures you incur a deficit. If you do not pay your deficit the national debt rises.

If you have to service the national debt you do not have money for social programs. Now how can a member honestly oppose revenue increases and expenditure reductions when he knows the ultimate result of that opposition is destruction of the social programs which those revenues support?
Let me give a concrete example of that. In 1984 when the present government of Canada took office the national debt was $200 billion. It rose in four years to $350 billion, a difference of $150 billion. Eighty per cent of that increase was compounded interest. In other words it bought Canadians nothing; it just satisfied the creditors of the government. Billions of dollars were literally thrown away, not available for street children, not there to help education, not there to provide medical services because we were paying it out in interest. Yet members opposite say, "continue that policy, carry on with that policy, pile up deficits".
As a result of the actions of the government over the last four years the expenditure program was reduced by $25 billion on an annual basis. In 1984 the expenditures of the Liberal government of Canada exceeded revenues by $16 billion. This fiscal year the revenues will exceed expenditures by $9 billion, which is an exchange of $25 billion. If we add that amount to the current deficit, already too high at $28.5 billion, it would be in an astronomical deficit figure of over $50 billion. What would that do to Canada? What would that do to social programs? What would that do to medical care and what would that do to post-secondary education? Yet that is what the members opposite advocate.
April 24, 1990

I am surprised that the people of Canada are taken in by this obvious disinformation by opposition members to people across Canada. Why are they taking it in? It has joined the New Democratic Party in militating against financial responsibility at the national level. They are going to destroy the jobs of their members and sooner or later the members of the Canadian Labour Congress are going to see this point and ask what their leaders are doing to them. They are undermining their future.
If there is not a strong national economy there will be no jobs for Canadians whether they are trade unionists or otherwise. The only basis for a healthy economy is a balanced national budget and that is undeniable.
That is why on February 20, 1990, the Minister of Finance introduced his budget. That is why we took the measures that we feel are necessary with respect to transfer payments.
For example, Established Programs Financing is a program whereby the Government of Canada supports education and health care across Canada for all Canadians. The expenditures rose 6.3 per cent. What happens when expenditures increase by 6.3 per cent on an annual basis and the government of Canada is keeping its own expenditures increase at 3 per cent?
That is a great sacrifice, of course, to public servants and to all Canadians through the tax system because Canadians are paying more money for this financial responsibility. Public servants are receiving less in increases and that is their sacrifice.
The New Democratic Party does not want any sacrifice, just to carry on with the programs that have been enforced. The former Liberal government established a policy of buying votes with people's money and they do not want it to stop. They say that we do not need these measures.
Surely their conscience is telling them otherwise and surely they recognize that the rhetoric they preach in this House of Commons is destructive to the country. What does it take to bring them to their senses, if dollar bills on a chart do not tell Canadians exactly where we stand? Do they really want us to go down the road with Brazil?

I tell members to be honest in the House of Commons and with the people of Canada. Join with us in letting the people of Canada know that we have a financial problem in 1990 and we can solve it. Mr. Speaker, Premier John Buchanan's offhand remark last week that joining the U.S. might be the best of a sad set of options for maritimers in the event of a separate Quebec set off a storm of predictable protests. Opposition Leader Vince McLean responded in a predictably partisan and hysterical manner.

Mr. Speaker, rural Canada is in a state of severe crisis.
In western Canada seeding is just beginning, and in two weeks it will be in full swing. Not only are thousands of farmers facing the loss of their farms, but many are facing the prospect of being unable to put seed in the ground. Yet to date, there is nothing in place to assist farmers, and ensure that their crop will be planted.
In my riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, like elsewhere, there are many farmers in severe trouble. One of them is Amie Taylor. Mr. Taylor lives near Kenaston and for almost 20 years has been operating a mixed family farm. However, this year the banks have refused to lend him any money to put in his crop.

Mr. Speaker, last Sunday I attended a special service in Scarborough with over 1,000 Canadian Armenians to remember the brutal genocide which began 75
years ago today in which over one and a half million Armenians were massacred in the Ottoman Turkish empire.
There were several survivors who escaped the genocide at Sunday service. We owe it to these survivors and we owe it to those who lost their lives to officially recognize that a genocide did indeed occur.
Can you imagine the Jewish people of this world being told that the Holocaust of the Second World War during which six million Jews lost their lives did not occur? In closing, it is time for Canada and other democratic countries around the world who value human rights to set the record straight and recognize the horrific genocide of one and a half million Armenians which began in 1915.
