Mr. Speaker, today is the seventy-fifth anniversary of the Armenian genocide. From 1915 to 1922 more than 1.5 million Armenians, half the population of Armenia, died in pogroms whose efficiency Hitler imitated.
Throughout history, and even today, Armenians have been subjected to racially motivated violence and murder. As part of their heritage language and cultural program, students are taught the importance of remembering and fighting for justice, freedom and democracy in Armenia and around the world.
In metropolitan Toronto and throughout Canada people have learned to appreciate the courage in adversity and leadership and industry of Armenians as well as the tragic human suffering and waste caused by racism.

Mr. Speaker, I know very well the Canadian Armenian community. For more than 26 years, relations of friendship and mutual understanding based on our common features have developed between that community and the rest of Canada.
I can assure you of the great loyalty of the Armenian community in our institutions in Montreal, Quebec, and in Canada as a whole. Today is a special day because we mark the 75th anniversary of the genocide of 1915, a day which reminds us of very painfull events.
Turkey should admit its responsibility in that genocide, just as the current leader of the Soviet Union recognised
the role played by his country in Poland and in other similar tragedies.
As always, we sympathize with our Quebec and Canadian friends of Armenian origin and we wish them a better future, while hoping that soon, Canada will submit the matter to the United Nations. Shenorhagalyem.

Mr. Speaker, this past Sunday was International Earth Day. We witnessed people all over the world demonstrating their commitment and concern for the fate of our earth. People participated in international events and they did so on a volunteer basis. They cleaned parks, sorted garbage, planted trees and did whatever it took to demonstrate their desire to be part of the solution.
This week is National Volunteer Week. It is indeed a good time to recognize the good work many volunteers contribute towards improving our environment. We encourage them for we need their help. We applaud them for they are the backbone of our communities.

Mr. Speaker, the corporate welfare bum of the week award is back. This week's three nominees are Magna International, which got a tax credit of $8.2 million on profits of $19 million in 1988. The second nominee is PWA, which did not pay any tax on profits of $30 million in 1988. However, it did find $250 million to buy Wardair in January, 1989. The third nominee is American Barrick Resources, which paid no taxes in 1988 on a net income of $30 million. And the winner is: American Barrick Resources.
While it did not pay a single penny of federal income taxes, this large corporation did have $4.6 million to pay its chief executive officer, Mr. P. Munk. Mr. Munk obviously earned this huge salary for his accounting prowess and for helping American Barrick Resources to be the corporate welfare bum of the week.
April 24, 1990

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, petrochemical companies in Sarnia-Lambton continue to undertake initiatives which illustrate that the environment is rightfully becoming a number one priority.
In February, Nova Petrochemicals announced two voluntary improvements in its local manufacturing facility to improve its environmental performance. A new environmentally-friendly cooling water treatment process was initiated which virtually eliminates low-level discharges of chromium and zinc from its final effluent.
Also modifications to the flare stack have facilitated more efficient use of steam in the safety system and significantly reducing the amount of smoke emissions during flaring activities.
I applaud these efforts by Nova in its pursuit of environmental responsibility and consciousness. I strongly encourage other interests, private and public, to demonstrate a comparable commitment to our most valuable finite resource, our environment.

Mr. Speaker, the financial challenges facing resource-based industries today are appalling and almost insurmountable. One of the industries that is suffering the most as a result of the policies of this government is the forest industry.
The sad part is that today we have a government that is more interested in listening to its own rhetoric than it is in listening to small business and the people of Canada. The forest industry is suffering because of the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber. It is suffering because of the increased value of the Canadian dollar in relation to the American dollar. The forest industry, like many other businesses and consumers, is suffering because of high interest rates.
I call upon the government, and Canadians call upon the government, to get rid of the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber and to take growing interest rates and the value of our dollar seriously in order to put what once was a thriving industry back on its feet again.
Oral Questions
Failure to do so demonstrates in realistic terms that we have a heartless and inhumane government.

Mr. Speaker, National Consumers Week is a way to ensure that the various market interests- consumers, companies and governments-become fully aware of its operations and their respective responsibilities. Indeed Quebec has given us an outstanding example of business and government co-operation designed to provide consumers with up-to-date information. The Montreal regional office of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has prepared a food labelling guide. With the support of Laval University and a number of private sector interests, Mr. Pierre Blais, Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and member for Bellechasse, has launched today, with participating companies, a campaign to distribute about one million copies of this guide.
Mr. Speaker, this is just one example of the way consumers, companies and the government join forces to promote a more active market place.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday, John Allan, Chairman of Stelco, one of Canada's largest manufacturing firms, announced that his company is cutting 800 jobs across Canada. Mr. Allan said the impact of the Bank of Canada's high interest rate, high dollar policy is, and I quote, "adversely affecting our domestic markets for steel, while making it more difficult for the steel industry and its customers to export their products".
In light of this statement by one of Canada's key business leaders, is it not time for the government and the Bank of Canada to stop this high interest rate, high dollar policy which is so damaging to our basic manufac-

April 24, 1990
Oral Questions
turing industries and the people working in them? How many more thousands of jobs will be lost before the government comes to its senses and stops this policy of high dollar and high interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, I take no comfort in the announcements that the Chairman of Stelco made yesterday. I do not like to see people laid off. I do not like to see companies having difficulties doing business.
What I do understand is that, if we ignore these problems, companies like Stelco are going to have a much more difficult time in the future as they did in 1981-82. At that time the government ignored the seriousness of the inflation problem. The problem got out of control and led to the very serious difficulties that Stelco and others experienced at that time. That was a very tough lesson for us all to learn. We have learned from that lesson, and we are going to avoid that problem this time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously Mr. Allan does not agree with the minister. Yesterday, Mr. Allan, president of one of the country's major steel companies, also said, and I quote: "If the present monetary policy goes on for any great length of time, the tradeable goods-producing element of the economy will suffer very serious and permanent harm".
I therefore want to ask the minister why he insists on maintaining this monetary policy of high interest rates and a high Canadian dollar, when it proves to be a real threat to the health of our economy. Why?

Mr. Speaker, I guess what the hon. member is asking me to do is to engineer a drop in interest rates. If we had a reduction in interest rates at this time, with the inflationary wage and price pressures we are facing today, that will lead to higher inflation down the road. That is the very thing that Mr. Allan is concerned about, which is, according to the quote of the hon. member, "a more permanent loss in their competitive position". We want to avoid that more permanent loss in the competitive position of Canadian industry by getting the inflationary problems under control now, so that we avoid the runaway inflation that we had when inflation was not 5.5
per cent in the 1980-81 period. It was 13 per cent. That 13 per cent led to interest rates of 20 per cent to 25 per cent.
Surely, this is something we should be trying to avoid. We are doing everything we can to avoid this problem right now with this government's policy.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the minister will not listen to me or Mr. Allan, one of the leading business people in this country, perhaps he will listen to his own colleague, a senior member of his caucus, the member for Mississauga South and Chairman of the Finance Committee of the House of Commons. The chairman said yesterday, and I quote: "I think the monetary policy is totally wrong." I repeat the quote: "I think the monetary policy is totally wrong."
If the minister does not want to listen to me and he does not want to listen to the leading business people in this country, why will he not at least listen to the Conservative Chairman of the Finance Committee and drop his high dollar, high interest rate policy, about which even that chairman says: "is totally wrong"? Why not?

Mr. Speaker, if my friend is saying that the member from Mississauga South is so correct in everything he says, why does he not accept the position that he has taken with the GST? My friend from Mississauga South said that is exactly what we should be doing as a government.
I listened to these self-righteous statements on the part of the member from Windsor West where he says we must be doing this. I ask him to consider back to what he said, as I reminded him again yesterday, prior to the 1980 election. He was put on the spot by Morton Shulman. He asked: "If interest rates go up after the election, what will you do? Will you resign?" The hon. member said that, yes, he would resign.
Mr. Shulman asked him a second time: "Are you sure you would resign?" The Hon. Member is shaking his head. I have the TV clip and I can show it to him sometime. Mr. Shulman asked: "Would you resign?" a second time. A second time, he said: "Yes." What happened when interest rates went to 20 per cent and 25 per cent? This self-righteous member sat firmly in his place, right there in the House. He did not resign.
April 24, 1990

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the President of the Treasury Board.
Yesterday's report, Beneath the Veneer, shows the inequities imposed upon women in the Public Service of Canada. The Canadian International Development Agency is a world-recognized authority in programs eliminating just such discrimination. Can the minister tell us when he will implement CIDA's Social and Gender Sensitization Program in Canada's own public service?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like once again to thank very much Jean Edmonds, Edna Mackenzie and Jocelyne Cote-O'Hara for having done a very good piece of work in producing the report.
The report is the first of its kind, giving us very detailed documentation about some of the problems that exist and that we suspected existed when we appointed the task force. It defines these problems.
I can tell my colleague that the report is being acted on as of today. We are not going to hold up action on this report. We are making sure that senior managers are aware of the report, the recommendations and the problems. We will be giving a comprehensive response in a very short time.

It all sounds veiy pretty, Mr. Speaker, but CIDA has had something very close to the answer since at least 1986. It is a program that has been successfully implemented in India, in Nepal and in Australia. If it works in Australia, it should work here. There is even a handbook to implement this program, written at the Cote International Institute at the Prime Minister's own alma mater.
When is the minister going to use the solution at hand, and use a Canadian program to benefit Canadian women?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize the fact that this Task Force on Barriers to Women in the Public Service followed upon a number of initiatives taken by the government to improve career opportunities for women in the federal public service and to dismantle barriers.
Oral Questions
I would like to say that among positions directly controlled by the government-for example, in the deputy minister range-we increased the percentage of women in that group from 8.5 per cent in 1985 to 16.7 per cent. For the Governor in Council appointments, the rate of increase was from 21.8 per cent to 36.3 per cent. In the senior management category, from 1984 to 1989, we went from 6.7 per cent to 13.1 per cent. We will continue. We have been working on this issue for the last five years and we have been doing very well.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who seems more intent on giving a history lesson than trying to explain to Canadians what is happening in 1990.
There are certain realities that the minister is going to have to face about his high interest rate policy. One of those realities is that we have lost 71,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector since November, 1988. Another one is that, with the cut-backs of 800 jobs in Stelco, business leaders increasingly are saying that the high interest rates are destroying business in the country.
This minister cannot deny that interest rates have gone up 20 times since the last election and that his interest rate policy is driving Canadian business into the ground. It is driving businesses into bankruptcy and putting workers on the unemployment line. Why does the minister not address his high interest rate policy and admit that it is not working?

Mr. Speaker, I do point out to the hon. member that in the last three months employment is up by 64,000. That is the increase for the total in the economy. My hon. friend can be selective about her statistics, but those are the total economy statistics.
She asks why I am giving a history lesson. The only point I am making is that it is important that we learn from history. It is important that we look at what happened in comparable periods in the past, learn from the mistakes that were made at that time-and there were a lot of mistakes-and try to avoid making those mistakes now.

April 24, 1990
Oral Questions
My hon. friend says the anti-inflation policy is not working. I ask her to consider what the inflation rate would be if we had kept interest rates down and we had a lower level for the Canadian dollar. We would have inflation up in the 6.5 per cent to 7 per cent, or maybe higher, range. That is what we are trying to avoid with the policies that we are following.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians have no faith in the projections of the government, a government that projected an 11 per cent interest rate and had a budget based on that 11 per cent interest rate which had nothing to do with reality.
Last week, the Consumer Price Index indicated that inflation is increasing at least partly because of high housing costs related to the high interest rates. It is obvious that the government's high interest rate policy is increasing inflation, not decreasing inflation.
I ask the minister again: Will he admit that this high interest rate policy is, in fact, increasing inflation and not decreasing it?

Mr. Speaker, if we go back to projections, I remind her of the projections made by her predecessor in 1984 and 1985. When we brought in our economic policy at that time, the hon. member for Oshawa, Ed Broadbent, said we were going to see 150,000 to 200,000 job losses. In fact, it was quite the reverse. We saw 150,000 to 200,000 jobs gained as a result of the policies we had been following.
My hon. friend talks about housing starts. Housing starts over all in the country today are about 220,000, around the level they have been at for the last four or five years. We still have a good degree of strength in different parts of the economy.
My hon. friend asks whether the policy is working. If we had not followed the policy that we are following today, we most surely would have higher levels of inflation. It was those higher levels of inflation back in the 1970s which brought the 20 and 25 per cent interest rates at that time.
Is that what my hon. friend is calling for? Does she want to see 20 and 25 per cent interest rates again? That is what we are going to avoid as a government.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Canadians want to see some responsible economic management. Ask farmers, ask Canadian business people, ask consumers about the rate of interest and ask them what their faith is in this minister's policies.

The Minister of Finance is aware that every time interest rates go up, the deficit goes up as well.
With the kind of interest rates we have today, the deficit will increase by three and half billion dollars next year.
This country needs full employment, a lower deficit, a lower rate of inflation and social services. Will the minister finally admit that his interest rate policy defeats all those objectives?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says she wants higher employment and lower inflation. I do not know how she is going to get that lower inflation if she wants lower interest rates. Lower interest rates are designed to increase inflation. That is the effect.
So is the GST.

Now she is talking about the GST. Let me ask her this question. Why is it that the New Democratic Party is against the GST when it will lower the cost of doing business for the farmers in this country by $240 million? It will lower their cost of doing business and lower the cost of food that they will be able to sell to the wholesalers and the supermarkets.
This is what will bring about lower inflation as we get the GST into place. For the life of me, I do not understand why the NDP is against the farmers of this country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I never said yesterday that there will be no stop-work order. I said that I will be pleased to announce today that this government has the intention to comply with the judgment so as to strike a full panel review of the whole dam project.

Mr. Speaker, safety may not mean much to somebody sitting in the middle of Ottawa, but it certainly means a lot to the people of Alberta.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the task force report on barriers to women in the Public Service was released. It documented the incredible barriers women face when they are trying to escape the pink ghetto.
Women who were sexually harassed were told that they had no sense of humour or they were given negative appraisals. A woman was told by her boss that if he were her husband he would beat her black and blue. A systems analyst was told: "You're not an engineer, you're just a stupid woman". A woman who had run her own electronics shop was asked in an interview: "Do power or hand tools scare you?"
My question is for the Minister responsible for the Status of Women. When will her government show the leadership that is necessary to change this situation? What is this government planning to do to eliminate these barriers to women in the public system and when will it do it?

da has no say over an indirect transaction between two international companies that took place in London. speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not only in the hon. member's riding that the Community Futures Program has been helpful. The chairman of the Economic Recovery Commission in Newfoundland is quoted as saying that the Community Futures Program has been very helpful in rural development in Newfoundland. In the riding of Gander-Grand Falls, held by an hon. member across the House, the Central Newfoundland Community Futures Committee is working on a number of programs to bring about economic development.
Under our labour force development strategy, when we get our new legislation, which we would urge hon. members opposite to urge on their colleagues, it will be possible to increase by one-third, $50 million, this wonderful program for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. The minister will know that the much heralded Environmental Protection Act is a shockingly poor example of action. Last year only a paltry 3 per cent of polluters were charged after being
Oral Questions
caught breaking the law. There is only one lonely inspector for all of Ontario, while this government will hire 4,000 people to make sure the ordinary Canadian complies with the tax rules.
How can the minister tell Canadians he is taking action on the environment when the facts prove otherwise?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that environmental efficiency must be measured in terms of people being put into jail. We must do much better than that.
As we all know, the regulations enacted during the Liberal regime did not allow the government to lay charges under the legislation because it is said in the regulations that they do not apply to mills built prior to 1971 and more than 90 per cent of mills in Canada were built before that date. This means that we must update those regulations to be in a position to lay the charges where we have to.

Mr. Speaker, the International Joint Commission says that the health of kids is threatened by the toxins of the Great Lakes water. There were 5,000 chemical spills, three times the number made public before. The clean-up program gets only $25 million this year, while the GST gets $111 million of a $1.5 billion total.
How can the minister justify spending billions on taxing Canadians while the environment gets shafted?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government shares the concerns of the hon. member. The Secretary of State for External Affairs met his vis-a-vis in the American government the day after the tabling of the report to discuss that. I met Secretary Reilly last week to discuss the same things.
We think we must upgrade the efforts of the two governments to deal with this great problem.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for Canada Post. Earlier today the Conservative members of Parliament recommended in a report to privatize all rural post offices, to sell to the private sector all of Canada Post, and to increase prices and services to

April 24, 1990
Oral Questions
provide for a dividend of 40 per cent to the Government of Canada.
Will the minister stand in his place now, totally dissociate himself from those propositions and commit himself to a modem, efficient and publicly owned postal system for Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to stand in my place and applaud the excellent work by this committee in recognition of the tremendous progress that Canada Post has gone through in the last few years.
I understand the rate of return recommendation to mean that the true costs of delivering the mail, including the cost of capital, should be borne by the users, 80 per cent of which are businesses.
Is the hon. member suggesting that it is a good economic and social policy to have these business users of the post office subsidized by the general taxpayer by providing for less than the real rate of return on the money invested by the taxpayer?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister.

The Postal Services Review Board, the consumer watchdog, was abolished in the last Budget, ostensibly to save $3 million annually. Since Canada Post spends $17 million eveiy year on advertising to convince us it delivers the mail, is the minister now prepared to allocate at least $3 million of this money to protecting the consumer?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the protection of the consumer is well served by an efficient and effective post office that delivers the mail within the time limits that consumers expect.
It is obviously always difficult when you have to cut back on government operations, like the Postal Service Review Committee. It was difficult because we have this monstrous deficit which we inherited from previous governments and which we are trying to manage.
In a competitive world advertising is how you reach your customers. The post office has customers. It must advertise, along with its competitors, in order to serve its customers. The hon. member believes in state control in a socialist type of operation where advertising is unnecessary. We don't.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who will know that less than two years ago Canada organized and hosted a major landmark international conference on the atmosphere, now known as the Toronto Conference.
During that conference international scientific consensus was achieved that we need to reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 20 per cent by the year 2005. Canada agreed to that. The scientists and politicians who were there realized and publicly stated that our problems with the atmosphere are just as serious, if not more so, than the threat of nuclear war.
Is Canada's word good, less than two years later, that we will reduce our carbon dioxide emissions by 20 per cent or more by the year 2005?

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Bouchard (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's word is good. The day we make a commitment it will be fulfilled.
We must make a serious commitment to know to what we are committed, and to know what will be a burden on the citizens.
As the hon. member knows, we are waiting for the most important report of the IPCC, a UN body, which will be tabled in August. And there will be a major conference in Geneva in November.
After that, there will be targets and schedules for S02 reduction in The Green Plan for Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

Just for absolute certainty for the Canadian public and for this House, Mr. Speaker, I would like to get an assurance from the Minister of the Environment who said that Canada's word is good.
When he says that Canada's word is good, does he and the Government of Canada mean that Canada will live up to a 20 per cent reduction of carbon dioxide emissions

based on 1988 levels by the year 2005? Is that what the minister meant?

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-69
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is it because members of the government consider cutting services to poor Canadians, to sick Canadians, to Canadians living on the streets and dependent on food banks to eat an issue of such principle that they refuse to debate it? Are they afraid to debate the cutbacks they have made to the provinces in our social programs, our hospital and medical programs and our post-secondary education? Doctors in the province of British Columbia are crying out for help. Patients are crying for help to be served within the hospitals.
I believe that closure is being used to rush yet another unpopular measure through this House. None of us should be surprised. This is the same government that kicks out its own members for speaking their minds.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-69
speechtext: Gave them the boot.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-69
speechtext:
That is right.
They are not fooling any of the Canadian people. The public knows the score with this government. They have been telling Angus Reid and Gallup what they think of this government for years.

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
I am sure there are many members opposite who read the polls that I have referred to who think that they are living a nightmare. I want to tell them they do not know what a nightmare is.
A nightmare is sleeping on a bench in Vancouver because you cannot afford to support yourself. A nightmare is lining up at a food bank to get the minimum amount of food to keep your family going for another day. A nightmare is not being able to receive basic health care or education because this government has cut transfers to British Columbia. Between this government and its counterpart in Victoria the people of B.C. have received a double whammy.
The nightmare of the people of B.C. and, indeed, all the people of Canada will end the day this government is tossed out of office. That is a day that I can assure members opposite is not that far off.
I want to talk a little about accountability. During the last election Progressive Conservative candidates talked about accountability. I would like to talk about that accountability now.
Between 1980 and 1984 when the Liberals were in power, the then Minister of Transport was trying to bring about some changes to passenger rail service and make cutbacks to those services.
I travelled across Canada at that time with the present Deputy Prime Minister. He sought to save the rail system then. Yet when this government brought forward a measure to cut VIA Rail services he never said one word to protect them.
Where is the accountability in this government when it comes to hearing what the people have to say? Where is the accountability when it comes to the goods and services tax? Where is the accountability when the cutbacks come?
During the last election campaign the Prime Minister said that our social programs would be well protected. Yet today we have a situation in which transfer payments to the provinces are going to be capped and cut back- when the Prime Minister stated that they would be protected.
There is no accountability on that side of the House. Canadians are sick of a government that subsidizes corporate entertainment to the tune of $1 billion a year
while the lines at the food banks continue to grow longer.
Canadians are sick of a government that asks lower and middle-income Canadians to pay for the debt that it has created. Canadians are sick of a government that would rather argue with physicians through multimillion dollar television commercials paid for by the taxpayers rather than on the floor of the House of Commons.
Literally millions of dollars are being spent to promote the goods and services tax which this government is trying to impose on the Canadian people. However, when we want to argue to protect the social programs, the hospital programs and post-secondary education programs in my province of British Columbia, we are not allowed even to debate them.
This government can continue to invoke closure. It can continue to cut programs to those most in need. I would like to leave the government with one thought. In 1992 or thereabouts, the Canadian people are going to institute closure on this government. I can assure you of that, Madam Speaker.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are debating a motion of time allocation concerning Bill C-69. Such a motion concerning other bills, as well as closure, has been debated more times since December, 1988 than almost any other issue that we have talked about in Parliament.
In his remarks this morning the member for Halifax West stated that we have known about Bill C-69 since it came forward in the February 20 budget. He said that because it was in the budget all Canadians know about it. As far as I am concerned, that is not the case.
As the member of Parliament from the riding of Hillsborough I believe that I and every other member of Parliament in this Chamber should have the right and the time to discuss the issues that are very important to their ridings and, indeed, to their country.
Under the EPF the federal government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all the provinces through the transfer of tax points and cash pay-outs. The transfers were to assist provinces in their responsibilities in health care and post-secondary education. Over time, and after many meetings with representatives in both health care and educational fields, the message that has
April 24, 1990

been reiterated is that the provinces need more money to function, not the same amount or less money.
Since the government came to power in 1984 it has on three separate occasions reduced the amount of federal transfers to the provinces for medicare, hospital services and post-secondary education.
The impact of these cuts on Prince Edward Island alone up to 1995 will mean a loss of $155 million. For every man, woman and child in that riding it means a cost of close to $2,000 each. In turn, the spin-off of these cuts once again enters the millions of dollars.
The government tries to fool the people by saying that the richer provinces of Alberta, Ontario and British Columbia will be receiving less funding, therefore leading us to believe that the poorer provinces will be receiving more funding. However, that is not the case.
Education is the lifeline of Canada's future. However, this government continues to cut back on funding to students and post-secondary educational institutions. Each year as the population increases and more students realize the necessity of an education the demand for classroom space is increased, while the number of instructors per students will decrease if the funding for the extended budget is not there.
As our health care system advances we find people living longer lives and the rising cost of high technology medical equipment placing a further burden on the system. Now what we have are two essential systems. As the member for Gander-Grand Falls said this morning, there are two systems in this country that should never be touched when we come to cutbacks, belt tightening and restraint. They are health and education.
Now, instead, we have these two groups pitted against one another for funding due to the nature of the allocation of the funds. If the provinces now decide not to increase taxes, they will be forced to make cutbacks. In turn, the hospitals will have to close beds, limit costly operations or find other reductions.
On the other hand, students will face higher tuition fees. In the outlying regions, the Atlantic region and other regions of Canada, not only will students face the high cost of tuition fees but in those areas where
Government Orders
seasonal employment and low paying jobs are the norm the problem will be to find a job at which they can earn enough money to see them through their education. Now, with the costs being higher, this will be even much harder to do. They are going to face overcrowded classes, or other cost-cutting measures.
I now want to reiterate a statement made by the Minister of Finance on March 24, 1982, when he said: "Let us not make hospitals, universities and colleges a battleground between the federal government and the provincial governments. Let us solve those problems, not on the backs of the hospitals and the universities. Let us solve those problems outside of that arena."
We are all aware that the deficit is a very serious and a very real issue. However, the deficit cannot be passed from the federal government to the provincial governments, causing further burden on the various regions across the country. The Atlantic region, as we know, has seen tremendous reductions in federal government financing over the past year, and it will be particularly affected by these moves.
In my riding of Hillsborough, a great many people are on a fixed income or are seasonally employed. I would like to stress that they are seasonally employed not by choice or by laziness. Now they face the possibility of another burden around their necks, that of the GST in 1991.
With the government now transferring its debt we will see an increase in both municipal and provincial taxes, adding further insult to the injury of my constituents. Municipal governments are already facing increased burdens with the decline of municipal infrastructures across the country. They cannot afford to deal with the costs associated with the federal government passing the buck.
The government must begin to negotiate with all the provinces regarding regional planning and to consider the growth factor across the country and the need to upgrade all our facilities in all of the provinces. In doing so, it must propose a framework for the progress of the nation in order to ensure equal access for all Canadians to educational and health care institutions.
I would like to conclude by saying that Prince Edward Islanders are fully aware of the deficit problem Canada is

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
facing. We are more than willing to do our fair share. But, as I speak, our share is growing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you very much.
Before rising to speak to Bill C-69, I checked a few figures. I found that the number of times the government has used closure is absolutely phenomenal. In the Thirty-fourth Parliament alone, we have seen some 17 times that the government has used closure, as well as an additional five times for time allocation. When we consider the number of sitting months we have been in session since the election of November 1988, that is approximately twice per sitting month since then. It has been invoked almost once every two weeks.
One begins to wonder just what kind of mind-set exists in the government. Maybe, in the beginning, in those cases when the government considered that members of the opposition were taking extra long lengths of time over some of the serious issues it had brought before the House in the last year and a half, it was necessary. But, it became a habit and the guillotine fell time and time again. I do not know how many times it has happened since the new government House leader assumed his role. He should have been watching the French Revolution on television recently. The use of the guillotine here and the axe falling again and again makes me think that the new government House leader is the Maximilien de Robespierre of the Conservative government and the Whip is Saint-Just.
The government should bear in mind what happened to those people. People who bring the axe down time and time again, in order to deny legitimate dissent, and in order to disallow legitimate dissent from having an opportunity to fully express itself, will end up being the victims of their own weapons.
Members of the government like to say-and I have heard several of them say it in this debate, the few of them who have spoken-that one has got to make hard political choices. They say: "We have to cut somewhere". They say that they have to make choices about what they are going to spend, what they are going to cut, and that there is only so much money going around.
I want to remind them that on the day prior to the last budget they brought in a bill-I believe it was Bill C-52-which was voted for unanimously by all members of the Conservative party and by all Liberal members of the Official Opposition. The supposed purpose of that bill was to reform registered retirement savings plans. But the effect of that legislation, supported by both the Liberals and the Conservatives, was to pass on large tax savings, totalling some $300 million to $350 million per year, to the sole benefit of Canadians who earn over $86,000 per year. That same legislation took away benefits from Canadians who earn under $40,000 per year. They made their choice then.
I mention this because the reasoning of some members amazes me. One of my Liberal colleagues, as reported in The Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, April 5, said: "Let us have no illusion about what this bill is about. It is a tax bill to help the rich". That was the Liberal member for Willowdale who, assuming he was here at the time, voted in favour of the legislation which he says is a bill to help the rich at the expense of the relatively poor.
The government has made its choice and members of the opposition made their choice. The government says now that we have to go along with cuts to women's programs, drastic cuts through tax increases to municipalities, and radio licence fee increases of up to 1,800 per cent in some instances in my own locality. It says that it must cap the Canada Assistance Plan to the detriment of people on social assistance, those who are at the bottom rung of Canadian society economically. It will hurt our health care system through cuts and the freezing of revenues under the Established Programs Financing.
For the government to claim that this is necessary, while just days before the last budget it handed over one-third of a billion dollars to those Canadians who earn $86,000 and up, is more than mischievous. It is a betrayal of the people it is supposed to represent, the majority of its electorate. Those people did not benefit
April 24, 1990

Government Orders
by this action taken the day before the budget. Those people are going to be hurt by the legislation that is before us today.
It is no pleasure to take part in a debate like this. But it is a responsibility that we have to take seriously to point out to the government again and again that it must begin to be consistent. If it has to make cuts, then make cuts to those who can afford to be cut. Do not attack those least able to defend themselves, while at the same time rewarding those who do not need the help of any of us.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to be recognized. I rise today to speak on Bill C-69 and the disastrous effects that the cutbacks in established program funding will have on the various areas of Atlantic Canada that are concerned.
The two major areas of my own riding of Halifax, my own province of Nova Scotia and my region are of course those of post-secondary education and health care. I spoke briefly in the time allocation debate regarding the necessity of matters such as this having a full airing, and that the duly elected members of the opposition being permitted to do their job and represent the attitudes and the beliefs of their constituents in a debate as important as this one is. Consequently, I am delighted that I will be one of the few who will have the opportunity to make remarks in this particular area.
The government has launched a massive assault on funding for post-secondary education. The combined effect of the freeze, the 1 per cent reduction in the EPF funding after the freeze expires and Bill C-96 and Bill C-33 will result in almost $9 billion less in post-secondary funding by 1995. This is an estimate prepared by the Canadian Association of University Teachers.
Given the fact that education is the future and the hope of Canadians nation-wide, what we are seeing is a withdrawal from and a refusal to recognize the fact that this sort of program is the only sane kind of investment in our future that Canadians want to see, need to see and have a right to see. I speak from the heart when I talk about the plight of universities in Atlantic Canada. A number of my colleagues across the way will know that I speak correctly. I speak about universities such as Dal-housie, Mount Saint Vincent, Saint Mary's, the University of King's College, the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design, the Technical College of Nova Scotia, all of which are in or close to my own riding of Halifax.
I speak of St. Francis Xavier University in Antigonish, Nova Scotia, the alma mater of a number of members of this House, both past and present, not the least of whom, of course, is the Prime Minister of Canada. I speak of Acadia University and College Sainte Anne in Pointe L'Eglise in Nova Scotia. I speak of the other university that, although it is in New Brunswick, is considered under the funding rules to be partially Nova Scotian. My learned colleague from Cumberland-Colchester will know that I refer to Mount Allison University. And I speak of the University College of Cape Breton. All of these universities have a number of things in common. The first thing they have in common is a high standard of excellence in the training and education of students and in the level and devotion of faculty members. The second thing they have in common is a deteriorating physical plant and an inability to pay their faculty members up to the scale of other universities in this country. We are all aware that the farther west you go in this country, the higher salaries are for faculty and staff and the lower tuition rates are for students. Indeed, Nova Scotia boasts-if I can use that word-the highest tuition rates in the country and the majority of Atlantic students can ill-afford to pay those extremely high tuition fees.
These universities have in common the fact that their boards, faculty and students work in buildings that are long in need of major repair. They use laboratory facilities that are considerably behind those available to universities in the rest of the country. The fact that we can still compete at all with those researchers south of the border is absolutely amazing.
April 24, 1990

The tradition of education in Nova Scotia is a long one. All of the people who make up the founding peoples of the province of Nova Scotia have had a long-time belief in education, in cultural pursuits and in developing the best possible technology to keep our province in the best possible industrial and developmental patterns.
I go back back to the habitation at Port Royal in 1605 of the first Europeans in Nova Scotia. They founded the first social club in North America of which we are very proud in Nova Scotia. The social club is known as the Order of Good Cheer. One of the things that is not known is that the Order of Good Cheer was one of the first play writing schools and theatrical endeavours in North America as well. Indeed, the settlers at the habitation were encouraged by Champlain, de Monts, and de Poutrincourt to produce plays that related to their own situation in Nova Scotia back in the early 17th century.
Madam Speaker, that is a proud tradition. I hope that sometime you will come to Nova Scotia and we will be able to bring you into the Order of Good Cheer.
I bring up this particular story to shed light on the things happening in our universities. They are happening nation-wide, but particularly in Atlantic Canada, because of the massive cutbacks. The universities are being forced to justify their existence in the light of technology, in the light of preparing people specifically for jobs which relate to the more technical side of education. As it is, with that change in direction, they are still hamstrung to a great degree by this cutback in funding, none more so than in the science, medical and engineering faculties.
On the other side in education, the humanities and arts side-and I know that this is something that is dear to you, Madam Speaker, as well as it is to me- is where we really see people losing out. We see those faculty members trained in literature, in theatre and drama, in music, in the lively arts. The money is just not there. It cannot be raised to keep those faculties going and to perpetuate a tradition of Canadian culture of fostering young writers, dancers, actors, directors, choreographers, and so on. All participants make our country and
Government Orders
its cultural life such a tremendous mix of all the peoples who came to Canada and settled here. That is a tragedy.
Beyond that sense of funding for universities being cut off in the lively arts area-the theatre schools, dance schools and so on-we also have the other areas of the humanities.
I can remember finishing my first degree in 1970, an Honours BA in English, and being told quite rightly that I was fit for nothing. Nobody would be prepared to pay me for anything I had learned in the past four years, which was perfectly true. Fortunately, I went on to further education at that point.
We all know that the employability of the average arts graduate in the country today is probably comparable to that of a high school graduate 20 years ago. I do not think anyone would disagree that if our universities are being forced strictly into the technological mode, strictly looking at training people for the job market and for nothing else, we lose another major piece of our soul. I cannot think of another word for it. Those of us who spent the time studying the supposedly arcane areas such as literature, philosophy, languages, logic or whatever, may not have been able to come out and operate computers. We may not have had technology at our fingertips, and, indeed, as I was told, many of those people are being told: "You have no skill that is marketable."
Educating in that area keeps alive and vibrant, in a country such as ours, the spirit of all our various cultures. The fact that people still study and still want to go on and teach in areas that are not particularly lucrative and that are not considered the high point of the technocratic age, says something for the commitment that Canadian academics and Canadian students have to the other side and to the theory that a person-man or woman-cannot live by bread alone.
As we see the cutbacks to Established Program Funding, we are going to see that universities will just not have the luxury of expanding, let alone not cutting back on English, drama and philosophy departments. I have nothing against computers and there is no one in this Chamber who could survive without them. But young Canadians, when choosing career paths and given the choice between a degree in computer science and a

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
degree in English literature, French literature or philosophy, are obviously going to say: "Computer science."
On the other side, the pure science side, our universities in the Atlantic are dealing with equipment and laboratories that are 20 years out of date. In my university, Mount Saint Vincent, the only women's university in the British Commonwealth, we have just recently, with the consent of the former Speaker of the House, Madam Sauve, established a Jeanne Sauve Chair for Women in Science.
From my years as a faculty member in that institution, I can tell you of the dedication of women and men in the areas of chemistry, physics, and biology, in particular, who laboured to teach and to teach to the maximum of their ability. They laboured to bring to their students the latest developments in a physical plant that again was 20 years out of date. With the establishment of the Jeanne Sauve Chair and with various other fund-raising techniques that are going on, that situation is being slowly changed. But the moneys that might have gone into improving the situation in science faculties at our only women's university, with the cutbacks to EPF, are probably going to have to be spread more thinly across the whole university. Indeed, there are going to many other shortfalls that will be found there, as at the other universities that I mentioned.
It is unfair and short-sighted that we take this cut. There is no question, and I am sure that many people will bring this up as we go on in this debate, that there is a deficit in the country and that the deficit must be handled. We have all discussed the varying ways that the deficit could be handled. My colleagues much more knowledgeable in the area than I am.
The hon. member for Gloucester, among others, has spoken frequently about what a 1 per cent drop in the interest rate would do to the deficit. We know that, by cutting back 1 per cent in Established Program Financing, we are saying to thousands of young Canadians: "I am sorry, but a university education, a post-secondary education, or a specific educational program that will make you a better trained Canadian and give you a better outlook on life and a better start when you come into the
workforce is not going to be available to you." Universities are going to have to close classroom space. They are going to have to let faculty members go and they are going to have to cut back. There is just no other way. The only other possibility from that is that tuition fees would reflect the actual cost of educating a university student.
The actual cost of educating a university student in Canada today is, at minimum, $10,000 per year. How many Canadians in 1990, parents or students, could look at the possibility of post-secondary education and say: "Yes, I can afford $10,000 per year for tuition." This is without talking about how much money it is going to cost for living that year in university, how much money will be needed for books and transportation. With the cost for books, one must now add in the 7 per cent GST as well.
If we do this, we again become closer to the so-called model for the government, that being the United States. The majority of universities in the United States do have tuition rates that high and even higher. They have a different system there. They have endowments and scholarship funds and they have a population 10 times the size of ours to draw on. Even with that difference, the ideal of a university education in the United States of America is still one that belongs almost exclusively to the upper middle class. In the supposed land of the free and home of the brave, south of the border, it is not an opportunity that every child has. Indeed, it is an opportunity that only belongs, in general, to the well-to-do or to those who manage to achieve an academic level that is probably beyond the vast majority of high school graduates.
In Canada, the children of fishermen, coalminers, steelworkers, prairie farmers, Ontario factory workers, Quebec factory workers and fishermen, and loggers in B.C. have always known, in the post-war society, that a university education was within their grasp.
I ask the government, as it brings this bill to the vote, is this what it wants? Is this the memorial to this government that it wants, along with the GST, the end of VIA and a variety of other perfidy? Does it want people to stand up and say: "It was the Mulroney government that ended the dream of post-secondary education for the vast majority of Canadians." I hope not, but I fear so.

Perhaps a history of Bill C-69 and the matter we have before us would be of some interest to those who will some day read what we are discussing today. Bill C-69 was introduced in the House of Commons on March 15 of this year. Its purpose was to implement key aspects of the expenditure control plan affecting statutory programs proposed in the February 20 budget of the Minister of Finance.
Combined with the restraint initiatives announced in December 1989, this plan will reduce government spending by an estimated $3 billion in 1990-91 and $3.8 billion in 1991-92. The federal deficit is projected to decline from $30.5 billion in 1989-90 to $28.5 billion in 1990-91 and to $26.8 billion in 1991-92.
April 24, 1990

This bill affects four programs: the Canada Assistance Plan, the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program, the Established Programs Financing arrangement and the public utilities income tax transfer. I would just like to focus on a couple of these.
First, the Canada Assistance Plan. The federal government pays the provinces half the cost of eligible social assistance expenditures under the CAP. These transfers have grown from $4 billion in 1984-85 to about $5.5 billion in 1989-90, an average annual increase of 6.7 per cent. The amendments do not affect provinces which receive federal equalization transfers. The federal government will, therefore, continue to share half of all eligible expenditures incurred in these provinces.
For provinces not receiving equalization, the bill provides for a maximum of 5 per cent annual growth of CAP contributions for 1990-91 and for 1991-92.

The provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia are in a much better financial position than the federal government to finance expenditures beyond the 5 per cent growth rate. The implementation of this measure will provide for resumption of the present regime on April 1, 1992.
I would like to focus some attention on the Established Programs Financing. The EPF is the single largest transfer program to provinces and has grown from $14.5 billion in 1984-85 to almost $20 billion in 1989-90, an average annual increase of 6.3 per cent. Under EPF the federal government provides equal per capita financial assistance to all provinces through the transfer of tax points and cash payments. Historically these transfers were undertaken to assist provinces to carry out their responsibilities with respect to health care and post-secondary education. Since 1977 provinces have been able to use these transfers according to their particular priorities rather than in a more restrictive fashion required by the previous cost-sharing arrangements.
The bill will hold the per capita EPF transfer in 1990-91 and in 1991-92, to its 1989-90 level. However, total EPF transfers will continue to grow with the population increase of each province or about 1 per cent nationally. The bill provides for a resumption of EPF

growth in 1992-93 at the rate of growth of GNP less 3 percentage points consistent with the announcement in the April 1989 budget. The growth of the total EPF transfer beginning in 1992-93 will not fall below the rate of inflation.
This change in the EPF will have exactly the same per capita impact on all provinces and represents less than 1 per cent of provincial revenues in 1990-91. Low-income provinces will continue to benefit from large and growing equalization transfers which have been exempted from the expenditure control plan.
Bill C-69 is a major component of the budget that was announced in February as we made earlier reference and I think it would be of some interest at this time to make reference to how the impact of Bill C-69 relates to the budget and more important how our budget affects our country.
Our budget is about building for the future, not borrowing from it. That is why our budget deals firmly with the major obstacle to that future, the problem of our growing debt. The measures in our budget reflect the seriousness of the debt situation we face and at the same time we have worked to ensure that the total package of measures is balanced, reflecting regional circumstances and placing the greater burden on those who are better able to carry it.
As a government we are acting with a resolve to reduce expenditures and to improve our own efficiency and operations. All Canadians are being asked to play a greater part in dealing with the debt problem.
Let me outline the actions we are taking to deal with this debt. We are reducing government spending affecting a wide range of programs from national defence to government operations. As a result of these and earlier actions program spending, relative to the size of the economy, will continue to decline significantly. By 1993-94, it will fall to its lowest level in a quarter of a century.
The budget measures will cut the annual deficit in half to $14 billion by 1993-94. As the deficit goes down the debt will shrink as a proportion of our national income. Interest costs will take less of every revenue dollar. Our healthier fiscal position will help to reduce inflationary pressures and thus create an environment favourable to lower interest rates. In this way the fiscal actions in this

April 24, 1990
Government Orders
budget make an important contribution to achieving sustainable economic growth.
To achieve this goal a period of moderation and demand is also essential. Indeed, economic growth is expected to moderate and to average about 1.3 per cent at an annual rate for 1990. Employment will continue to grow during this period, however, but at a somewhat slower rate than labour force growth.
Over the medium term inflation and interest rates are expected to decline and the economy to resume growth at its potential rate, averaging about 3.5 per cent a year. If we had not acted, we could have faced a growing danger of higher inflation and even higher interest rates that could have led to a severe recession.
For the longer term we will continue to build a foundation for economic progress by moving forward with a balanced agenda of fiscal and economic action. The replacement of the existing federal sales tax is a key element of this strategy to safeguard essential programs and strengthen Canada's economy. The government will proceed with reform of the federal sales tax effective January 1,1991, certainly no surprise to you. This reform is expected to result in major gains in economic output in the range of about $9 billion a year, gains that will be felt in all sectors of the economy and in all regions of Canada.
I would like to comment about the effects that this program has in total for our federal government support for education. We deem education to be an important priority. That is why the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers agreed in a November communique that they would work together to examine ways of allocating resources more effectively with a focus on results through the proposed new task force on Canada's human resource development system.
On January 30 the Prime Minister told the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology that to improve Canada's competitive position and I quote: "We must control the deficit and the debt if we are to unshackle our hands". That is what the budget and Bill C-69 are all about.
Students of today are going to be major beneficiaries of the improvement in our fiscal and economic position in coming years. As part of our broad-based efforts to get us out from under a growing mountain of debt we have introduced Bill C-69. Among other things it will
hold constant for two years per capita entitlements under the EPF financing arrangements, which is the government's largest transfer to provinces. Historically, these transfers were undertaken to assist provinces to carry out their responsibilities in respect of health care and post-secondary education.
Since 1977, provinces have been able to use these transfers according to their own particular priorities rather than in the more restricted fashion required by the previous cost-sharing arrangements. In any case, transfers under EPF will remain large at over $20 billion in this year alone.
Together with equalization assistance to the lower-income provinces, the federal government will make available over $28 billion which provinces can draw upon. Federal support for education is broader than transfers to provincial governments. It includes many programs that are not affected by the Budget or Bill C-69.
These include research funding to granting councils of over $700 million this year. There is about $40 million for the innovative centres of excellence program and there is available funding of $17 million for the Canada Scholarships Program. There is about $250 million for the Official Languages and Education Program, almost $25 million for the literacy program, over $700 million for education services to native people and over $400 million for Canada student loans. There is also a large and growing amount of support for training and labour-market initiatives under the new labour force development strategy.
I would like to comment on the effects of Bill C-69 on my home province of Saskatchewan. The EPF financing transfer to Saskatchewan will be limited to the same per person levels as in 1989-1990 for the next two fiscal years. Equalization transfers, which are of great importance and in Saskatchewan are nearly 60 per cent of the size of the EPF, are expected to continue to grow with the national economy, which is much faster than other federal spending.
Growth of social assistance transfers to Saskatchewan under the Canada Assistance Plan will also be unaffected because the budget exempts provinces that receive equalization from the 5 per cent cap on the growth of these payments. The result is that transfers to Saskatchewan under these three major programs, which in
April 24, 1990

1989-90 totalled $1.23 billion, are expected to rise in the next two fiscal years to $1.25 billion and $1.29 billion. While these increases are less than they were projected to be prior to the budget, they still represent average growth of about 2.4 per cent over the next two years. Federal support to Saskatchewan is going to continue playing a strong positive role in the provincial fiscal picture.
On a per capita basis, the federal transfers are expected to amount to $1,236 for each Saskatchewan resident in 1990-91 and $1,269 the subsequent fiscal year. The comparable figures for Ontario are $956 and $963.
One of the major criticisms that I have received with respect to the attainment of office is the fact that we as a government must continue to keep our shop in order, keep our program spending under control and in fact to effect cuts. There is a feeling that we are not capable of doing that but for the record I would like to go through as many of these as time permits to explain how this government has in fact responded. That response may not have been made with the bells and whistles that would attract the eye and the ear of the average ratepayer but nevertheless we have been quite effective.
We have provided three elements to approaching a program of fiscal management. First, the government has taken action to cut the growth in spending on government programs. Second, the government has acted to increase its revenues. Third, it has put in place a policy framework which is revitalizing the private sector and will permit sustained economic growth.
Economic growth is essential if the Canadian economy is to generate new wealth and new income. This includes, of course, the Free Trade Agreement, tax reform, deregulation in the energy and transportation sectors, privatization and measures to encourage new investment.
The government previous to our election increased spending by an average of 15.1 per cent a year. This was cut to an average of 5 per cent during our first four years. Excluding interest payments on the public debt, the previous government increased spending by an average of 13.9 per cent a year and we cut this to an average of 3.6 per cent a year during our first four years in office. After accounting for inflation this means that program
Government Orders
spending has fallen, on average, by half a per cent a year in real terms. In comparison, the previous administration increased program spending by an average of 5.2 per cent a year, and above the rate of inflation. Oh, but to have that freedom, that reckless abandon.
Spending has grown at a rate that is considerably less than the rate of the growth in the economy. As a result, expenditures have fallen from 24.6 per cent of GDP to 22.2 per cent last year. Spending will further decline to 20 per cent of GDP by 1993-94. Program spending has fallen from 19.5 per cent of GDP to 16.1 per cent and will fall to 15.2 per cent by 1993, back to the level of the late 1980s.
The cost of operating government, that is salaries, equipment, maintenance, et cetera, is actually less today than it was five years ago. But this does not mean the government has not acted to introduce new initiatives to meet new priorities or to deal with short-term problems such as we responded to with respect to the drought in western Canada. We continue to offer $.5 billion on a matching basis to assist the continuing dilemma that exists in agriculture today.
A further initiative we have undertaken is the privatization of 16 crown corporations. The government has improved its cash management and its use of resources. For example, the public service has been cut back to the size it was in 1973. Members of parliament have themselves set an example by receiving average annual salary increases of only 2.8 per cent over the past six years, a rate that has been considerably below the rate of increase in the average industrial wage and in the inflation rate.
Many projects have been cancelled, including the Canada Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program, a savings of $180 million and $315 million, respectively. The position of ambassador to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization in Rome was cancelled along with five other small posts. The $3.1 million Petroleum Incentives Program terminated in March 31, 1986, with an annual savings of some $600 million in 1986-87 and $1.7 billion in subsequent years. The list goes on. TV studio production services available to all members were discontinued with annual savings of some $300,000. AECL's two heavy water plants on Cape

We have cancelled programs and projects in response to those people who have written to us requesting that in fact we tighten up on government spending, subsidies, and assistance programs which perhaps were not as readily available as at the time the programs were initiated.
In the area of privatization a number of crown corporations have been sold since 1984, generating revenues for the federal treasury and also producing savings on operating costs. Madam Speaker, believe it or not I do thank the hon. member for the question. I know her well, and know the spirit in which the question was asked.
First of all to clear the record, I never was at any time President of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. I should have been, I thank the hon. member. I did come very close to being on that elite group because I did sit on the executive.
The hon. member said that as a municipal politician I had a certain perspective and now that I am federally positioned, my position seems to have changed. She wanted to know how that happened. I would like to advise the hon. member and the House that my perspective has not changed a bit. During the time that I was the
April 24, 1990

Mayor of Regina it was our goal as dictated to us by the responses of the citizens of Regina to be fiscally responsible.
During the last three years that I was in office, we effected a zero per cent increase in the rate of our own financial expectations in that we made political heroes out of ourselves by having a mill rate increase of zero for some two years. Another year, it was below the rate of inflation.
We did that anticipating that we would receive continued growth from our other two favourite sources of funding, namely the federal and provincial governments. When that does not happen then we as municipal politicians have every right in the world to scream, kick, holler and blame others, because certainly we do not want to take the blame ourselves. Whatever our role, we fulfil a function that is rather infallible. Of course, as a result we would not take the blame.
With respect to Bill C-69 we as a federal government have simply followed the budget, and proceeded with an intense and serious program. It is an extremely difficult path to follow because we know it is not a popular one. On one hand we get reams of mail from people telling us to be fiscally responsible and on the other hand we have an opposition telling us how cruel we are because we are cutting funding.
We are not required to cut funding. We are not required to increase taxes. We are required to reduce interest rates and at the same time, keep control of inflation. If you put this entire collage together in the Mulligan pot stew I am afraid that it would not be palatable because one product would conflict with the other.
We are in a difficult position. I know the hon. member appreciates that, but given that she is a very patient person, she will wait until some day when she is in office when I will be able to ask the question. If I should have the patience that she has to be in opposition, should that period of time ever occur in the long life in which I wish to live, perhaps she will find the question as easy to answer as I did today.
