speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you know, this motion calls on the government to develop special initiatives in consultation with aboriginal people-and this is the key subclause in the sentence- to respond to the serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
This motion is extremely timely. It is one that deserves the fullest attention of the Government of Canada for a number of reasons. It is a well documented fact that aboriginal people have been mistreated in North America since Europeans came to this country.
In other words, aboriginal people have had a rough ride. No one can deny that historical fact. We know that in the early stages nations were massacred. We know that from time to time treaties were broken. We know that reserve lands, on some occasions, were poor in resource, poor in location and poor in size. We know that there have been cases of forced relocation. I know of the case of one band near Chicoutimi which, between 1920 and recent months, was relocated seven times to accommodate the exploration ambitions of a mining company.
We know that the earlier European settlers brought with them diseases, infections and certain social habits which proved to be devastating to the aboriginal people. We also know of denial of rights, the most recent one in the proposed Meech Lake Accord, which has been the object of persistent and consistent objections on the part of the native people, and understandably so. Meech Lake is not designed, structured and written in a manner that meets the approval of our aboriginal people. On the contrary, it has been objected to strenuously.

April 24, 1990
Private Members' Business
We know also that there are certain parts of Canada, most notably British Columbia, where treaties do not even exist. We know also of megaprojects that were put in place in the 1970s, as in the case of James Bay, where development destroyed the native way of life.
Today, as we debate this matter, we know that a second James Bay project is being proposed which would have a devastating effect on the lifestyle of the aboriginal people, namely, their ability to live off the land if, as proposed, substantial tracts of land are to be inundated and removed from their use.
In addition to that, as we all know, when forests go under water they develop a form of insidious mercury poisoning which infects the fish. This, in turn, has negative impacts on the health of the native population which consumes the fish. In other words, to sum it up, the impact of the white population and the white civilization has had negative consequences on the wellbeing of our aboriginal people.
It is true that now we can point to some signs of hope and it is worth while putting them on record. For instance there has been the negotiation of South Moresby on the part of the Haida nation; the work by the Lilloet tribal council, not only to try to save the Stein Valley but also to save their culture; the recent progress that has been made with land claim negotiations in the Yukon and Northwest Territories; and efforts by individuals such as Tom Henley who, through his rediscovery program, has attempted, and quite successfully so, to teach again to native youth their roots and their old ways.
Nevertheless, if one looks at the statistics produced by the Canadian Institute of Child Health last year prepared by Denise Avard and Louise Hanvey entitled "The Health of Canada's Children" and looks to the native population you will find some elements which justify the validity of the motion of the member for Nunatsiaq. They also make his motion one of an urgent nature.
For instance, Madam Speaker, if you look at the age composition of the registered native population in relation to the total Canadian population, you find that in 1985 nearly 34 per cent of the native population was less than 14 years of age, that is, slightly over one-third was below the age of 14. That compares with some 22 per
cent in Canada as a whole. That means, therefore, that the native youth population is larger by 50 per cent roughly than that of the non-aboriginal population. That in itself is a figure that commands the attention of this House and that of the government.
Turning to page 112 of that study under the heading "Suicide", we come across another set of figures which makes you pause and think. In 1984, the suicide rate for registered native teenagers between the ages of 10 and 19 was about seven times higher than the total Canadian rate. Suicide, as a footnote, is indicated as being of particular importance as a cause of death among young Indian adults.
Madam Speaker, obviously you would know, as would many in this Chamber who are familiar with social studies, that the suicide rate is of course a reflection and indication of the well-being of a culture to which that person belongs. It is not to be considered simply a disease or a temporary aberration. It is a very serious matter when it occurs, even in small percentages. However, here we are talking of a rate that is devastatingly high, namely seven times higher than that of our non-aboriginal population.
I ask myself what is the root of this problem. You are indicating to me, Madam Speaker, that my time is up, therefore we cannot explore the possible answers to this question. I can therefore only stress to you, Madam Speaker, and to receptive members on the government side, the extreme importance and urgency of the motion by my colleague from Nunatsiaq and indicate to you that it would be extremely desirable that this motion be passed and made part of the policy of the Government of Canada because of its crucial and central importance.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a great privilege to rise in the House to speak on this issue. It is not the first time that the member for Churchill has had that opportunity. For a number of years I have risen in this House and talked about the very elements of this motion, the serious unemployment problem that is facing native people, the lack of facilities for education and the lack of real initiatives to provide adequate health care for native Canadians.
April 24, 1990

I wish to commend the member for moving this motion. It is a very important issue and it is good that this House is addressing it.
This is not a new problem. One of the things that has upset me about the debate in the last five years in this House is to hear Liberal members get up and pretend that the problems that native Canadians face are something new, that they are the result of Conservative government cutbacks, when that is anything but the truth.
We have had over 100 years of neglect of native Canadians. That neglect is coming home to roost. If you go into the communities of northern Manitoba, you see that they do not have water and sewage systems. If you go into some of the schools in those communities you will find holes in the floors. If you go into the nursing stations you will find that at any given time there is a 25 per cent shortfall in the required number of nurses for native communities in northern Manitoba.
That is something which can be found in all the remote areas of Canada. I am sure you will find the same thing in the Kenora-Rainy River riding, in the Territories, in northern Saskatchewan, in northern Quebec, in northern Alberta and in parts of B.C. So it is not an isolated problem. It is a problem that has resulted from years and years of government neglect.
The white paper of Jean Chretien of almost 20 years ago basically called for assimilation of the native people. It called for a cutback in direct federal government programs to native people so that they would be forced into the white society, forced to accept provincial government programs. The federal government program, the Buffalo Jump of the 1990s, was a restatement of that by the Conservative government of the day.
In this year's federal budget, money is being taken away from national spokesgroups of native people and those groups that have co-ordinated activities among natives such as the northern chiefs in my riding. If you take a look at those cuts you realize that the federal government is again going down the road of restricting the ability of native people to explain their needs to the Canadian population.
There have been years and years of neglect of government programs and now there is a concerted effort by
Private Members' Business
the government to make sure that the native groups cannot get their message across, not only to Parliament but to the Canadian population as a whole.
Let me give you an example of some of the problems that do exist. A study was done of the York Landing School in my riding. An engineer's report was prepared in March of 1988. There are 81 students in three rooms, three grades per room. The school is built of wood with no fire-retardant being added to the wood. Electrical panels are not covered. The fire alarm system does not work. The four-foot hallway between classes is used as a storage room. There is no library. There is no common meeting room. There are tools for a shop but no space to use them. There are no smoke detectors. The fire exit doors are stuck closed. That report was made two years ago. To date, there are no plans for a new school for that community. Each and every day, 81 students go to that school, a fire trap, a facility which should have been closed many years ago. That is not an isolated case. I can give you examples from throughout my riding, as I am sure can others in the House, of schools that are inadequate.
I see one of the former Ministers of Indian Affairs making a hasty retreat from the House. I can understand his need to do so.

speechtext:
Perhaps if the minister had done something when he was the Minister of Indian Affairs, we would not need to have this debate in the House today. The member for Provencher should know of what I am speaking because some of the communities of which I am speaking used to be part of his riding but are now, happily, part of my riding. Unfortunately, when he was the minister, schools were being built with the knowledge that in four or five years those schools would be over-crowded. In other words, there were young children bom in those communities who would not have a place in those classrooms by the time they got into kindergarten or Grade 1. That was the deliberate government policy for dealing with the school shortage in native communities across the country.
If you have ever been into a native community and looked at the conditions of housing, you would realize it

April 24, 1990
Private Members' Business
is appalling, Madam Speaker. We give money for native housing in remote communities that would not build a decent cabin for people in those northern areas. We expect them to live there with inadequate heating systems. We expect them to live in those communities, knowing full well that there are not proper foundations for their houses. We know the houses will start to rot in five to ten years. And that is what we call a housing program. One of the richest nations calls that an adequate housing program, and minister after minister of Indian Affairs has stood in the House and defended that type of program.
That same neglect and refusal to deal with the real problems can be found in each and every program that the federal government is responsible for with regard to native Canadians. We can talk about education, employment, economic development, medical services, water, and sewage. These are all important to native Canadians and we have a sad history of neglect.
Just this year, the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal again condemned our country for our treatment of native people. Again, we were reminded that a native youth has more chance of going to jail than completing high school; a very sad statistic. We know from other studies that have been made in this nation that our jails have a very high percentage of native Canadians; much higher than the 4 per cent to 5 per cent that they make up of the Canadian population. In many facilities, in areas where the native population is between 5 per cent and 10 per cent of the population, the native population within our criminal institutions is over 50 per cent. In some cases, it is approaching 75 per cent of the total population within those institutions.
Why does that happen? It happens because there is a real system of neglect in this nation. The neglect is continuing. This summer there will be fewer native people taking advantage of federal government programs for job creation because there is less money provided for those communities. One-third of the native youth who used to be employed through federal government programs in the past will be employed this year. That is despite the fact that there is a growing native population. We are taking away their hope and, as long as we take away their hope, we take away their future and we taint our own future.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank you very much for recognizing me at this point. My colleagues, I am sure, will have other things to say as we go along.
With regard to the topic today, the report of the Special Senate Committee on Youth, tabled in 1986, states: "native Canadians have suffered from injustice for many decades". A separate chapter was devoted to native youth. It was found that unemployment among young natives was alarmingly high, as were pre-marital pregnancies, alcohol and drug abuse, suicide and problems with the law; in fact, more so than with other youth groups in our society. It became apparent that in order to address these problems the entire context of the historical and present status of Canadian native people has to be considered.
One of the basic needs which has to be addressed is health. It is true that our natives are entitled to special health and medical facilities and programs. The very isolation and remoteness of their villages greatly reduces the effectiveness of adequate care. In addition to this, there are often problems of language and a distrust brought about by generations of rejection and struggle.
The problem, of course, is tied to the requirement of adequate nutrition. Isolated areas find it difficult to avail themselves of fresh produce, to name only one element of proper nutrition. The February 1989 issue of Canadian Family Physician carried a special feature on the nutritional problems of native Canadian mothers and children. Deficiencies were identified in Vitamin D among toddlers who suffered from rickets. It was noted that fluoride is not present in the water supply of most native groups, thus requiring particular attention in order to prevent dental caries.
Research indicates that expectant mothers show a lack of sufficient intake of calcium and Vitamin D. It stands to reason that, if native expectant mothers are not healthy, babies will not be healthy, and the statistics prove it. Infant mortality rates among the Inuit for the period 1983 to 1985 are much higher than Canadians for almost all categories. Sudden infant death syndrome is an important cause of infant mortality for Indians, Inuit and all Canadians. However, the rates for Indians and Inuit are higher than the Canadian rate. For Indians and Inuit, the post-neonatal death rate is higher than the
April 24, 1990

neonatal death rate, whereas, for the Canadian population, the reverse is true.
Significant nutritional problems still exist in the native Indian and Inuit population of Canada. Since eating patterns have changed for the natives, as well as for everyone else in Canada, studies show that native adolescents are also prone to eating junk food high in calories, fat and carbohydrates. Here again, an iron deficiency is noted among teenage girls. Changes have been noted during the last four decades in the way native communities nourish themselves. Poverty also plays a big part in the poor nutrition of mothers and children.
Professionals treating natives must be aware of their particular traditions, evolutions and present-day problems. Nutrition counselling must be made available by fully qualified native people whose advice might be more culturally appropriate. At any rate, all professionals should be well versed in the special needs of the native Indians and the Inuit.
It is a sad commentary on Canada that a country as rich as Canada, as the hon. member for Churchill said, sees so many of its citizens suffer because of malnutrition. A healthy body will contribute to a healthy mind. How can we expect under-nourished students to progress, to learn, and to develop to their full potential? Discouraged at an early age, many will succumb to drug and alcohol abuse and, unfortunately, to an early death, whether accidental or by suicide.
A study done for Canadian Social Trends, in the 1988 winter issue, indicates that suicide rates in Canada during the 1980s have been the highest in the history of our country. During the last decade, the suicide rate has been about double what it was throughout most of the period from 1921 to 1961-that is 40 years-and all well about previous record highs during the depression of the 1930s.
Sadly, suicide rates are especially high among native people. In 1986, there were 56.3 suicides for every 100,000 native men, almost 2.5 times the rate for all men, which is at 22.5. At the same time the rate for native women, which was 11.8, was almost double the rate for all other women at 6.4. The incidence of suicide is particularly high among young native men. In 1986, there were more than 100 suicides for every 100,000 native
Private Members' Business
men age 15 to 29. What a waste, Madam Speaker. What a waste of potential for our country.
I spoke earlier of the need for good nutrition to ensure a healthy, inquiring mind, and the danger for young native men and women to get discouraged when faced with lack of opportunities with the added burden of ill health. Unfortunately, their despair quite often leads them to worse health through substance abuse.
While detrimental to their health, these abuses invariably lead them to problems with the law, and here again they become part of the very high suicide rate experienced in federal penitentiaries and provincial prisons.
I think the time has come to review in a very special way the needs of our native and Inuit groups. It is time to give them a greater role in their own health and welfare services. It is time to prepare professionals for service and work in remote native and Inuit communities. Improvements to health and medical services do not automatically mean that we limit ourselves to only one area. Rather, I see improving the standards of living for native groups as an attitude encompassing a broad variety of social needs-health, education, social services and transportation. Within these headings the government should look at the related services. For instance, while considering better health services, attention must be given to dental health, nutrition, pre-natal and post-natal services.
The parliamentary Special Committee on Indian SelfGovernment, which was prepared by Mr. Keith Penner and his committee in 1983, agreed that "-ill health is not an isolated issue that can be resolved with more and better medical facilities. Through the exercise of Indian self-government, Indian people will be able to control the other problems to which ill health is linked- Jurisdiction over such areas as education, child welfare, and health is considered essential. By exercising control over these matters Indian people could ensure future generations are able to preserve and enjoy their culture and heritage".
The issue of native control has received a lot of attention and I realize, Madam Speaker, that planning is ongoing. But in light of the preceding statistics are we not left with the feeling that we must do more, and we must do more quickly?

April 24, 1990
Private Members' Business
Last year the Minister of State for Youth tabled a book entitled Hot-100 in which was listed an interesting array of programs for youth. Among the 100, several were designed for young Indians and Inuit. One in particular, the Indian and Inuit Health Careers Program, offers bursaries for those interested in pursuing a career in the field of health. I believe that this is a very worthy initiative, but maybe we could go a step beyond.
The criteria for the program says the program "will provide bursaries according to need". I would like to add to this that special funds should be put aside for visits to the student's community to relieve loneliness, to keep his or her interest current on local health issues, and to ensure that the students will not get discouraged and abandon their studies.
This is only one idea, Madam Speaker. As I mentioned before, The entire social fabric must be looked at. The entire needs and particular aspirations of the young Indians and Inuit must be taken into consideration.
My colleague from the Northwest Territories was not able to be here today to participate in this debate. I know that if he were here he would lend his voice to all hon. colleagues in this House.
He would be saying to all of us here that we must respond to the needs of our young native people. We must respond now if we are going to have any effect on their future well-being.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, am very pleased to stand in support of the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq.
The question that begs to be asked is this. What does it mean to be young, aboriginal and living in Canada today? The government's own documents refer to the economic disparities endured by aboriginal people in Canada. For example, the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy released by the government last summer states:
By all measures of socio-economic disparity, the 600,000 people who identify themselves as aboriginal continue to be the most disadvantaged group within Canadian society. Employment rates among the aboriginal working-age population have been about 45 per cent compared with 63 per cent for the non-aboriginal
population. Of those employed, incomes are up to a third lower than levels for employed non-aboriginal people.
Almost 30 per cent of aboriginal individuals aged 15 to 24 have less than a grade 9 education, compared with 7 per cent of their non-aboriginal counterparts. More than 76 per cent have neither completed high school nor pursued post-secondary education, whereas the corresponding percentage for non-aboriginals is 44 per cent.
The social costs of the high unemployment rates, and relatively low educational attainment levels, are enormous.
In the Canadian Human Rights Commission annual report for 1988 it was stated that Canada's treatment of aboriginal peoples is a national tragedy. In its 1989 annual report the commission said it had no reason to alter that judgment.
The government is simply not doing enough. Aboriginal issues should be a priority. A focus on aboriginal youth is critical.
According to the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy:
For at least the next 15 years, the aboriginal share of the young labour force, which is 15 to 34 years of age, will be rising, reaching a level of 50 per cent higher by 1996. Most of this growth will occur in non-urbanized areas. Aboriginal people will account for 57 per cent of the increase in the labour force in northern Canada and 12 per cent in each of Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
For every year in the next five years, more than 5,000 individuals will have to find and keep jobs to achieve a level of 50 per cent employment among young Indian adults living on reserves.
Despite the fact that the government knows that half of the aboriginal population in Canada today is under the age of 25, and that these young people will need jobs, the government has not focused on these needs.
It capped the Indian post-secondary educational assistance program, limiting its accessibility. There is no initiative developed to respond to the serious employment needs of aboriginal youth.
In the area of health, serious inequities continue to exist in the area of aboriginal health. A recent report by the Canadian Institute of Child Health confirms the continuing problems.
The aboriginal mortality rate from injuries and suicides, hospitalizations due to respiratory diseases and pregnancy complications remain much higher than the national average.
April 24, 1990

Life expectancy is still much lower than for non-aboriginal people.
Aboriginal children born today will live, on average, 68 years. Other Canadian children can expect to live 76 years.
The aboriginal infant mortality rate is double the national average. Aboriginal children have consistently higher death rates due to injuries.
Aboriginal teenagers have a suicide rate seven times higher than that of the Canadian rate.
Tuberculosis and other infectious diseases affect aboriginal people disproportionately.
The government must come to grips with the Third World conditions that face aboriginal people and aboriginal youth in this country.
The aboriginal health, education and unemployment statistics are not acceptable and cannot be tolerated any longer.
The aboriginal people of this country want to contribute. The aboriginal youth want to contribute, but they need a fighting chance.
The circumstances which are currently blocking the opportunities for young aboriginal people have to be addressed as a priority.
That is all the motion the hon. member for Nunatsiaq is requesting. He is asking the government to pay attention to these serious issues. The government will say that it is already doing a lot. Whatever it is doing it is certainly not enough.
The frustration level of young Indian, Inuit and Metis people is rising. Current conditions do not offer them much of a future. Without dramatic changes they can most probably look forward only to unemployment insurance, welfare and an early death.
These young people deserve more from the federal government. We urge this government to respond favourably to the motion of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak in support of the motion presented by my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq. The motion states:
Private Members' Business
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider developing special initiatives, in consultation with aboriginal peoples, to respond to the serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
My relationship with the aboriginal community began about two years ago when I was beginning my campaign in Broadview-Greenwood. Many people would probably be surprised to hear that there are a lot of native people in downtown Toronto. Because of the frustration that native people experience when they are living on the reserves, they come to the city. Inevitably, however, when they are in the city they experience all kinds of rejection and frustration. They do not get proper employment opportunities. Because of that frustration they end up finding themselves out on the street. Social services are overburdened and they do not get the proper care.
It was during this period that I ran into Chief David Youngwolf from the Toronto Urban Indian Council. It was Chief Youngwolf who would tell me repeatedly of the frustrations that his people were having. That was the beginning of my realization that the native community of this country for some mysterious reason has not been looked at and appreciated in the way it should be.
We developed our relationship. Of course Chief Youngwolf's plea to me was this: "We are all going through a period right now where we care about the environment". Native people are really Canada's first environmentalists.
He worked with me for many months as we organized together the First Peoples Summit on the Environment. He brought his people in from all over Ontario. They put on displays and taught the younger children who came to this event from across the metropolitan area how to treat the land, how to work with the land. It was not just Chief Youngwolf, but many of his associates taught the youth the importance of having a healthy environment.
It was at that point in time that I realized that if we really are going to be committed to this environmental movement, we are going to have to treasure the resource of our native peoples.
When I realized this as time went on I went to the Minister of the Environment's book, which is obviously going to be the bible for this government come September. It is called a framework for discussion on the environment, and is entitled: The Green Plan: A National Challenge. I looked in the document to see if the minister

April 24, 1990
Private Members' Business
had recognized that the real environmentalists of this country are our native peoples.
Sure enough on page 14 I read:
Today's youth are tomorrow's decision-makers. If they are to play a meaningful role in environmental decision-making and diplomacy, they must develop environmental literacy as well as leadership skills. The Government proposes to take measures to ensure that Canada's youth will have the opportunity to channel their energy and talents toward achieving environmental objectives.
The Minister of the Environment then goes on to state:
The Government plans to support summer employment, training and career development in environmental conservation and protection, and to support international youth exchanges and conferences. Options include a federal government summer employment program; a private sector co-op program; and a youth conference in preparation for the 1992 UN Conference on Environment and Development in Brazil.
Canada's aboriginal peoples are often the first to experience changes made to the natural environment by human activities. Those changes have sometimes threatened their traditional and close relationship to the land.
I must say that when I read this today I felt like I was reading my colleague's motion. You will see the similarity, Madam Speaker. There are not more than 8 or 10 words missing. The Minister of Environment states further:
The Government will also consult with aboriginal peoples about other possible initiatives, including measures to support activities of natives that enhance or protect the environment and a special native component of the government's youth employment initiatives.
My colleague's motion was introduced in this House on November 27, 1989. I read that the Minister of the Environment has picked up on this motion. I am happy to see that. We can only hope now that the government will take these words and put them into action.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ABORIGINAL PEOPLES NEEDS OF YOUTH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am really very pleased to stand to add my voice to that of the member for Nunatsiaq, and all the other colleagues in the House who have spoken to the issue of his motion which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider developing specific initiatives, in consultation with aboriginal peoples, to respond to the serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
I think my colleagues have pointed out the serious situation that the aboriginal youth across this land find themselves in. Of course there are no magic solutions. It will take time.
There is no question that there must be a forwardlooking strategy. We must look at the kinds of issues that are ahead and ask ourselves: "Before we move to cut a program in this area, what are we doing to the lifestyle and to the future of the youth who are involved?"
It is really quite regrettable that with the challenges facing our young people in general, and our aboriginal youth in particular, that the government has chosen to cut community support programs that have often eased the struggle through these very difficult times. It has cut very important support mechanisms that we had built up in this country over many years which had helped the day to day realities of our aboriginal youth.
Far from enough, statistics indicate that we have done too little. Yet the little we have done has been cut. Once again, the government, unfortunately, has seen bottom line deficit reduction as the only yardstick of measure when looking out at society. If it had a constructive view of how to move forward, particularly in the area of our aboriginal youth who have serious educational and health problems, as well as serious problems with drugs and alcohol abuse, and in terms of the numbers in our jail system, I think the government would see that this is one area where we can ill afford to cut any funding or services.
I would say that I have been very privileged. I have attended the three First Minister's Conferences on Aboriginal Rights. I have seen outstanding leadership from the aboriginal communities, negotiating with the government in an effort to move forward their land claims concerns, to move forward their interest in picking up their society and their community and becoming more constructive and helpful in helping their own communities help themselves.
Those were very interesting but very frustrating conferences for aboriginal peoples. I appreciate their concern and their frustration in that regard.
April 24, 1990

I also sat on the legislative committee concerning Bill C-31 which looked at amendments to the Indian Act. It was very important at that time that we gave to Indian women equality of rights, the rights that their brothers and fathers enjoyed. I remember the argument in this House as we moved for assurances that money would be given for educational institutions when women and their children moved back on reserves. We sought assurances that more schools and homes would be built. In that way, their children would be assured of a better future. We all know that education is synonymous with an improvement of options and job skills training and an improvement in the future life of our children.
The statistics concerning youth in the aboriginal community are quite shocking. In that regard I would recommend to any one of my colleagues or people who are interested in the particular issue of the aboriginal peoples the speech of the hon. member for Nunatsiaq as reported in the House of Commons Hansard, Volume 131, No. 100, Second Session of the Thirty-Fourth Parliament of Monday, November 27, 1989. This is a subject that should interest us because the aboriginal people are the founding peoples of this country. Of any in our society, they are the distinct society. I think that this government has forgotten to include them in its major priorities.
The hon. member's speech is a most interesting, informative and somewhat sad critique of the way we have handled our responsibility as Canadians and as parliamentarians with regard to the place, role and importance of the Inuit and Indian people in the life of our country.
I would remind you as well, Madam Speaker, of when the annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission made those newspaper headlines with its grim statement: "An Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent to prison than of completing university". That is a statement that gives us food for serious thought and very serious concern.
In my critique portfolio of communications, one of most serious of the cuts comes to mind. I do not have to tell this House the importance of the communications media and how essential they are to the preservation of the cultural heritage of Canada's aboriginal peoples.
Private Members' Business
Broadcasting policy by itself, I acknowledge, will not ensure the survival of native language and native culture. But it can play a key role in helping to mitigate the threats that are commonly felt and the pressures that exist in a society. It can ensure a sense of belonging and participation. It can enhance that sense of roots that make people feel that they belong to a society and are reflected in that society.
That has an important role to play in the mental health and the well-being which comes with feeling that you have some knowledge of self, some place in your society, and that you are respected for the values that you have, as well as for the values that are promoted when one's image and one's place is acknowledged.
I believe -and that was certainly the view of the aboriginal leaders across this land-that the cuts put in place through the Secretary of State were unconscionable.
One of the things that I recall was that the then Secretary of State, the hon. member for Roberval, said: "It is particularly important that native people have access to communications, giving the aboriginal perspective during a time when such issues as self-government, aboriginal title and equality rights are being debated".
What did the government then do under the new Secretary of State, the hon. member for Pierrefonds- Dollard?
The Secretary of State cut the lines of communication to the people in their own language and in the manner which is important to the sense of importance and identity in terms of Inuit culture. I would say that the social culture and economic disaster that is brought about by the cuts to the native programs is totally unconscionable.
The CBC and native groups had begun to provide opportunities for aboriginal peoples to broadcast in their own languages. This came about, I would remind the House, through the establishment of the Northern Native Access Program in 1983, which provided support funds to stimulate the production of native language, radio and television programs. Outstanding programs have been produced.

April 24, 1990
Private Members' Business
When I was in Iqaluit I visited the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation. I saw incredible and creative programming. That is being cut.
All their newspapers are being cut.
If I had time I would list the areas of cuts that have left this native community in shock. I sincerely hope that serious reconsideration will be undertaken. The minister evidently set up a private task force, a hidden task force. Let him bring that task force report out into the open. It commenced at the beginning of March. Let him reinstate these programs which are fundamental to the well-being, both mentally and physically, of these societies.
I urge the government to reconsider its attacks against the native communications system which is key to their survival in their own society as well as to integrating them into the larger society, one which we then can appreciate as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wanted to say a few words but I did not want to do so without first determining whether I would be in that case preventing another member from speaking. But seeing no one else rise I want to take only three or four minutes before we adjourn to say a few words on this very important issue.
Madam Speaker, you know that I represent the native community of Cornwall Island, the Aquasasne Community No. 59, which is located in the great constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I thought I would take a moment to bring a few issues to the attention of the House in relation to the motion that was placed before us by our colleague from Nunatsiaq who moved the very constructive motion which states that the government should consider developing special initiatives, in consultation with aboriginal people, to respond to serious employment, education and health needs of aboriginal youth.
What is important in this motion, apart from everything else, are the words "in consultation with". The reason why I say that is because there is too much of what my colleague from Nunatsiaq has referred to as "big brotherism". That means that someone here in Ottawa designs programs for natives, as if all native Canadians live in similar conditions on reservations that are similar to one another and that they are all in climatic conditions which are similar to one another.
Of course, a native Canadian living in Tuktoyaktuk does not experience very many conditions that are similar to those natives living in the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell on Cornwall Island. That is important for all of us to remember.
I hope that through whatever program the government establishes, once we adopt the motion that is before us today, hopefully, we will ensure that we have this good and appropriate consultation, not just at the regional and national level with native Canadians, although we need that too but, indeed, at the local level so that programs are designed in such a way as to accommodate the various situations right across the country under which many of our native citizens live.
Needless to say, I have identified that a native Canadian living in the constituency of Glengarry-Prescott- Russell lives under very different climatic and other conditions than others do in certain other areas. But the social conditions and so on are very different as well.
We know of course that that particular community is located roughly one-quarter within the province of Quebec, one-quarter in the province of Ontario and one-half in the United States of America.
If you can, picture the following situation, Madam Speaker. Imagine that you are a citizen of that community and you travel between St. Regis, Quebec and Ho-gansburg, New York, and there are no Customs. If you travel between one country and the other there are no Customs duties, no Customs officers-no Customs anything.
On the other hand, if you live in another part of the same community on Cornwall Island and you go from there to Massena, New York, then there are Customs officers. That would be the same situation, Madam Speaker, if you were to leave Centre Block to go to the West Block and there were Customs, and there were no Customs if you went to the East Block and the East Block and the West Block were in the same country.
That is totally illogical in terms of conditions that people have to live under. It is only one element of conditions that my constituents live under which would appear to many of us as being not only very peculiar but in some cases nonsensical.
It creates various situations. We know that there is a problem with the illegal smuggling of goods through the reserve from the United States to Canada going through the American and the Canadian side of that community. That of course is most unfortunate. The Grand Chief of the Aquasasne reserve on the Canadian side has done his best and so has his council to eradicate this problem,
April 24, 1990

but it is very difficult. It is very difficult when you look at the high unemployment and the attractiveness that some might see in making a quick dollar that is otherwise not available.
When there are so few opportunities for those people one can see how some people could unfortunately be attracted to living off the avails of this kind of activity. It does not make it appropriate of course, and obviously the chiefs are very concerned and they are doing their best to stop it.
If we want to give other opportunities to those young people in Aquasasne, and elsewhere for that matter, we have to provide the necessary funding for a better education and better conditions.
It is my hope that we will adopt this motion today. I will leave enough time for us to be able to vote on this item.

Madam Speaker, I am standing here in the House today because a few weeks ago because I was not satisfied with a response to a question on veterinary services, the GST and how it would affect veterinarians.
Adjournment Debate
The Canadian Veterinary Medical Association and the Canadian Animal Health Institute both state that the proposed goods and services tax will have a drastic effect on veterinary services. In fact the firm of Deloitte and Touche on behalf of the CVMA studied the possible effects of the proposed GST on veterinary services and proved that small animal practices will face an increase in operational costs of more than 6 per cent. In some instances, due to administrative costs and cash flow problems, consumers may face up to a 12 per cent increase in veterinary care and drugs.
Because of these increased costs and cash flow problems, consumers may face up to a 12 per cent increase in veterinary care and drugs. Because of these increased costs, animal control programs will face a dramatic setback since spaying and neutering of small animals will inevitably decrease dramatically. Furthermore, we will see a decrease in health care provided to small animals, since consumers will not want to cover the increase in costs. This can have a drastic impact on not only the health of small animals, but also on humans because animals are carriers of many diseases that can be transmitted to man.
More than 50 per cent of Canadians have cats, dogs or other pets. Even if someone does not have a cat or a dog, one might be exposed to diseases such as rabies. One could be exposed to toxoplasmosis, which is transmitted through meat and cats and causes birth defects to the human foetus. One could be exposed to psittacosis, which is transmitted by birds and which can cause fatal meningitis. Therefore, the need to protect Canadians against parasites, fungi, mange, et cetera is essential, and an increase in the cost of veterinary services and drugs could deter many Canadians from making sure their pet is protected.
When I asked the Minister of State for Finance how his government could possibly justify putting the health of animals, and ultimately humans at risk, his response was: "The inputs presently paid by the veterinarians will no longer be paid after the GST is implemented. This will constitute a considerable diminution of the prices." This was said by the minister.
The CVMA and the CAHI both disagree with the minister's statement. In fact, Deloitte and Touche's study states that veterinarians presently pay the federal sales tax and also the telecommunication and program-

April 24, 1990
Adjournment Debate
ming services tax, at a rate of 11 per cent. Deloitte and Touche point out: "However, the removal of these two taxes will reduce the costs of operating veterinary clinics only marginally." This reduction in cost is estimated at less than 1 per cent.
Thus the minister is wrong. He is misleading Canadians. If the minister still stands by his statement, then where are his studies? Why not table them in this House?
The Deloitte and Touche report went on to state that there is no doubt that the costs of veterinary services and animal drugs to pet owners will increase under the GST as much as 12 per cent.
On a larger scale, veterinary services are essential to dairy and beef cattle breeders who have to resort to these services in order to keep their animals healthy and to protect them from contagious diseases. If this government taxes these services, it risks taxing the quality of food.
Veterinary services are essential to human health because in Canada there are veterinary inspection services in over 500 slaughterhouses and in food processing plants. As Mrs. Christiane Gagnon, President of the CVMA, told the finance committee last October, food such as pork, poultry, beef and eggs are checked by veterinarians, thereby ensuring the quality of safety of the food that we consume. Therefore, taxing those services boils down to taxing Canadian health.
In an August 1989 GST technical paper, the government stated that all health care services funded, in whole or in part, by health insurance plans in two or more provinces will be exempt under the GST. Even though governments in more than six provinces have established an animal health insurance plan, therefore meeting the stated criterion, the government has decided to overlook these facts.
Veterinary medicine is a medical profession and provides essential services to Canadians. Provincial governments and the federal government, have consistently recognized that animal health is essential to the health and well-being of all Canadians.
Furthermore, as I pointed out in my question to the minister, veterinary drug manufacturers were literally forced into complying with the Patent Act under which the whole pharmaceutical industry is regulated and under which no differentiation is made between human and veterinary pharmaceuticals. Nor has there been any
difference made between the two under the Excise Tax Act or under the Food and Drugs Act.
Now, under the proposed GST, human pharmaceuticals are zero rated while veterinary ones will be taxed, another prime example of this government's willingness to contradict itself over money. The CVMA points out that the inclusion of GST on veterinary pharmaceuticals will increase the costs of providing human health care and food products to the Canadian public as well as to the animal health care.
There will be both a direct and an indirect impact. Regardless of the fact that farmers can apply for refunds, they will be burdened with an increase in administration and financing costs. They could also experience increased product costs as manufacturers, distributors and veterinarians pass on their increased administrative or GST costs, through price increases.
The equal treatment of veterinary and human pharmaceuticals would ensure that price differentiation, due to the GST, would not promote the use of human pharmaceuticals and that adequate research and development continues on veterinary medicines.
The Canadian Animal Health Institute believes that the level of animal health care impacts directly on the level of human health care. Therefore, the differentiation of human and veterinary pharmaceuticals compromises the health of Canadians.
In conclusion, the statements made by the minister in reference to my question were unacceptable. The Canadian Veterinarians Medical Association, the Canadian Animal Health Institute and Deloitte and Touche have all refuted what the minister said in this House. They also refute comments by the member for Perth-Wellington -Waterloo.
When will the government listen to Canadians and scrap this unfair tax? Not only is the government grabbing money from Canadians, it is also risking the health of both animals and humans to do so. It is not too late to stop this madness and to scrap this tax grab.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to point out that, unlike the existing federal sales tax which applies to only one-third of all goods and services consumed in Canada, the GST will apply to most goods and services. This means that sectors across the economy will be treated more equitably, and that consumer
April 24, 1990

decisions will not be distorted as they are by the current system.
Consistent with this principle, veterinary pharmaceuticals will be subject to the GST. However, under the new system, all vendors of goods and services who charge GST on their sales will be entitled to claim a credit for GST paid on their businesses and inputs, that is, the goods and services acquired for the purpose of conducting their businesses.
Vendors of zero rated goods and services will not charge tax on their sales, but will be allowed to claim full input tax credits. In both cases, only the difference between total GST charged on sales and total GST paid on business inputs, will be remitted to the federal government. Moreover, when GST on purchases exceeds GST on sales, in the event, for example, of a large capital purchase, the difference will be refunded.
As a result of this approach, veterinary pharmaceuticals acquired by farmers and other commercial users will not be subject to the tax. This is because the GST they pay will be fully recoverable as input tax credits. Consequently the GST treatment of most veterinary pharmaceuticals will be effectively identical to that afforded prescription drugs for human consumption.

Madam Speaker, I rise to pursue several questions I have placed in the House concerning the court decision on the Oldman River Dam, but more broadly, on the implications of that decision and the ability of the government to exercise some genuine leadership and control over the environmental degradation of Canada's natural resources.
It is more than six weeks since that decision came down from the courts. It was a very strong decision. It made it quite clear that the federal government has not only the right but the responsibility to carry out a full environmental assessment of any project which impacts on an area of federal responsibility. It is unfortunate that it was not the Government of Canada that went to court seeking clarification of that right and that responsibility, and was testing the strength of its legislation to determine how far it could go in meeting the new imperative
Adjournment Debate
of Canadians to protect their own health and the health of their environment, through government action and government leadership. It was not in this case and the case of the Rafferty-Alameda Dam. It was private, independent, non-profit organizations that chose to stand up and fight for what the government refused to fight. It was a decision I thought the government and the minister would welcome as a green light to assume full responsibility for promises made to Canadians, and indeed to the world, at numerous international conferences, through protocols and press conferences. That is not what is happening.
The court stated very clearly and directly that the Minister of Fisheries shall carry out an environmental assessment, that the Minister of Transport shall carry out an environmental assessment. The federal permit to proceed with this project is cancelled. The government has chosen not to act on any one of those very direct orders from the court. It has chosen for over six weeks to answer repeatedly in this House that it is thinking about it. It is considering the implications and suggests that opposition members who raise the issue really do not understand the implications. Of course we understand the implications.
The first implication we understand is the contradiction between the words and actions of the government, which on the one hand states that it wants to act on the environment, but on the other hand not only fails to act, but refuses to act.
The government has several other challenges before it on which to take action. One of these is on the Point Aconi power plant in Nova Scotia. Again, it has been aware for some time of serious problems to the environment arising from this plant. It has simply sat back and let the process take its course. It has exercised no leadership on behalf of the people of Canada or on international commitments made on behalf of Canada to set targets for the reduction of emissions into the atmosphere.
The government has let the project go to the eleventh hour. It has allowed large amounts of money to be spent on preparing the project. It has not done what the legislation and the order in council states it must do, that

April 24, 1990
Adjournment Debate
is, carry out an environmental assessment early in the project, so it will know the environmental impacts and any mitigating measures can be taken. Once the project is approved, the design need not be changed, the project need not be interrupted and millions of dollars of investment need not be disturbed because work the federal government should have done in the first place was not done.
We face projects right across the country which clearly impact on federal responsibility. The government will have to decide to act. In Point Aconi, there is a request from the Coalition on Acid Rain for an environmental assessment. Will the government do as it did at the Oldman Dam and the Rafferty-Alameda Dam and refuse to carry out an environmental assessment which the order in council under that legislation mandates and, in fact, directs it to do? If it does, it is simply abandoning its responsibility.
It is now nearly two years into the discussion around the Carmanah Valley. The government has taken absolutely no action to examine the environmental asset of Carmanah, to determine what can and should happen to that environment in order to protect not only a unique Canadian resource, but in fact a unique world resource.
We hear the government talking about introducing its environmental assessment review legislation within a matter of weeks. I wonder how much effect that legislation will have, however weak or strong it may be, if the government refuses to implement a direct order of the courts to carry out environmental assessment. Will it in fact even obey whatever legislation it brings in? If it refuses to use the environmental tools now at its disposal, what hope is there that a new piece of legislation will make any difference? If the Minister of Transportation sits in the House as he did today and refuses to account for why he is allowing the project to go ahead without the federal permit that it legally requires under an act that is under his jurisdiction, then what hope do we have that environmental assessment review legislation will have any affect?
The minister knows perfectly well that a federal permit was issued for the dam to proceed and that that
permit has now been cancelled. For six weeks now that project has been proceeding illegally. Once again we are relying on private non-profit organizations to hold bazaars and fund-raisers to go to court to defend the laws of the land and not the Government of Canada. Yet the minister continues to ignore an illegal act.
If the minister is concerned about the safety of the project he has every opportunity to make public, as the environmental assessment review process requires, the safety implications. He has chosen not to do that so the public and members of the House can only question whether indeed, and what indeed, the safety factors are that allow and encourage him to over-ride the law of the land.
If he is concerned about safety factors he has the mandate under the act to determine how and under what conditions to meet those safety factors, He might issue a permit for the project. He has chosen not to do that because that, too, would be subject to public scrutiny.
We had the recent announcement of The Green Plan. The Green Plan was full of questions that I thought were answered a long time ago. The Prime Minister and other ministers of the government had this great Montreal-To-ronto conference and agreed to a 20 per cent reduction. However, that is not what is happening.
I simply call on the government to answer these questions for members of parliament and for the public. Are you serious about the environment or not?

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Forestry)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member raised a number of questions about the way the present government deals with its environmental responsibilities, and I would like to give a specific example to demonstrate that this government's activities are sensible and consistent. The Great Whale River project is a case in point. As you know, there is a serious problem, but for several months we have been talking to the Quebec government about ways of harmonizing this environmental review, since the project is subject to the environmental review requirements of both government.
April 24, 1990

Furthermore, considering the rights and privileges conferred under the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement on the Cree and Inuit people who live in this region, we intend to associate them directly with any process that will be put in place.
I must admit that we are currently up against some major obstacles to developing a completely integrated review process. The process itself must be independent and rigourous to be credible, a requirement that is difficult to reconcile with Quebec's exclusive jurisdiction over the project itself and with a project schedule that leaves little time for completing the required studies and reviews.
Nevertheless, recent Federal Court decisions leave us no choice. In fact, in addition to our own desire to apply sound environmental planning to the Great Whale River project, the Federal Court has handed down decisions that affect federal areas of jurisdiction involved in this project. Recent judgments in the Rafferty-Alameda and Oldman River cases stated that the court order on the guidelines for the federal environmental assessment and review process has force of law.
The court stated that a project is subject to public review under the guidelines whenever the federal government has decision-making power over environmental impact deemed to be non-minimal.
The court also emphasized the arm's length character of a public review board and the need for informing the public and providing the means for the public to participate and make its views knows in the course of the process.
The project is already subject to environmental assessment under the provincial processes provided by the agreement. The question arises whether these processes would not suffice. However, the emphasis on public participation and on the independence of review boards created under the federal order does not appear in the James Bay Agreement. Consequently, the Federal Court's decisions would seem to limit the possibility of using the agreement's processes while observing the requirements of the court order. If we want to meet the requirements of the order, we will have to set up a separate board, created under the order, or persuade the
Adjournment Debate
other parties to the agreement to accept a joint assessment process that maintains the essential elements of the order.
Our room to manoeuvre has shrunk considerably in recent months. This partly explains why it took so long to set up the requisite mechanisms, since we want to respect Quebec's requirements and harmonize existing processess in order to avoid duplication and be as effective as possible. However, we will have to do so in a way that is consistent with recent judgments by the Court.
If we are unable to reach some kind of agreement with Quebec, we will have to create an environmental assessment board under the federal order. The board would consider the concerns of Native people in relation to the Great Whale River project. In fact, we are convinced the Federal Court will force us to do so if we fail to meet our obligations under the court order on the guidelines.
In concluding, I repeat it is our intention to protect the environment of Arctic Quebec as well as the way of life and the rights of the Native people concerned, while respecting the legitimate desire of the Quebec government to develop responsibly its natural resources.
Madam Speaker, that was a good example of how the government and the Minister of the Environment see their responsibility with respect to environmental projects.

Madam Speaker, on April 6 in response to a question I raised concerning the impact upon the province of Prince Edward Island of changes the federal government has undertaken in its equalization payments which will cost the province some $18 million, the Minister of State for Finance told the House that:
The record of this government stands for what we think about the
poorer regions of Canada.
What has that record been? In terms of assisting the Atlantic fishery on December 13 of last year and again on January 22 of this year, the Prime Minister made some very specific commitments to Atlantic Canadians:
I have already indicated to my right honourable friend that the
government of Canada will act in respect of the Atlantic fishery with

April 24, 1990
Adjournment Debate
exactly the same kind of generosity and enthusiasms that we brought to resolving the problems of the prairie farmer.
That commitment was repeated on January 22 of this year. However, here is what the Minister of Fisheries told an audience of fishing industry representatives in Halifax on April 19 of this year. He said:
We are developing an adjustment, not an aid package for Atlantic Canada.
It is clear that Atlantic Canadians have been misled by this government. There is no aid package which will help communities to weather this crisis. The only thing the federal government intends to do is to provide Atlantic Canadians who have relied upon the fishery for generations a bus ticket to Toronto.
In two recent reports prepared by the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, a group which reports to the Minister of Employment, the impact of the government's policies toward Atlantic Canada were criticized.
In December of last year the council released a report on regional unemployment in Canada in which it stated:
For many regions, (he recession and its debilitating effects on individuals and communities is continuing to persist and some regions are still struggling to regain their pre-1981 levels of employment.
Later the council indicated that:
Among those involved with the problems currently being experienced in some regions, there is concern that Canada may actually be evolving into a two-tiered society-the prosperous industrial heartland and the depressed outer regions.
It should be kept in mind that this was a report written by an advisory council appointed by the federal government and is reporting on the situation it has found to exist five years after the Conservative government has been in office.
Contained in the same report is an assessment of the federal budget of April 1989 and the same comments with regards to cuts in the budget of 1990. That report states:
It appears certain that major negative effects will be experienced in some regions as a result of the following federal decisions: cut-backs in regional development funding, commitments for business development, forestry agreements, mineral exploration, transportation infrastructure, and oil industry megaprojects,
reductions in the growth of transfer payments to provinces for health, social welfare and education, changes to the UI program, closures of Canadian Forces bases, and lower subsidies for VIA Rail.
The Minister of State for Finance also told the House: "The unemployment statistics are the lowest they have been since 1981".
Again, the Advisory Council to the Minister of Employment stated:
'As far back as 1977 the Economic Council of Canada stated that 'Unemployment in some areas of Canada continues to be a national disgrace.' Now 12years later, this situation has not improved. In fact, it has become worse in many regions".
On March 28, 1990, the council issued a policy paper on the Atlantic fishery and the crisis which the collapse of much of it means. It stated:
Hundreds of Atlantic communities will lose their only industry. Predominantly in Newfoundland, there are few other jobs in these isolated settlements. Thousands of families, left without adequate incomes, will be forced to rely on welfare, or to uproot their lives for the dubious promise of mainland wealth.
The Minister of State for Finance said the record stands for what the federal government thinks of the poorer regions. It is obvious the government does not think very highly of those regions.
And what of the future? The Minister of Fisheries believes the best way to save the fishery is to destroy the lives and communities of many of those involved with it. Again, here is what the advisory council to the federal government says with respect to this attitude:
The unimaginative solution to over capacity and excess labour supply is to eliminate it. Reduce harvesting and processing capacity, and allow/force workers to move away. Additionally the cliche of diversification is trotted out as the ultimate solution. The result of these solutions would be the disintegration of the fishing industrial structure, especially in economically non-diversified areas, with chronic unemployment and the turning of many fishing communities into ghost towns".
Considering the vital importance the fishery has to the economic viability of the entire Atlantic region, how the federal government responds to this crisis will determine the future of the region.
If the indications given by the Minister of Fisheries in his Halifax speech are reflected in government initiatives, the future of many Atlantic communities and countless families will be placed in jeopardy.
April 24, 1990

Madam Speaker, in closing I have four brief suggestions that the government might follow to effectively deal with the problem of the Atlantic fishery and in fact would be a solution to put people first. This would resolve the problems faced by those who presently live in Newfoundland and who wish to. First, the federal government could begin to bring forth proposals to take control over the area of the nose and tail of the Grand Bank and the Flemish cap slightly outside the 200 mile limit.
Second, given the current crisis in the Atlantic fishery, they could intervene to ensure that a community based quota structure be put in place, even if only on a temporary basis to ensure that the fishing communities presently involved in the fishery can survive.
Third, the federal government must begin to enforce or take seriously its responsibility for the management of the fisheries and accept the financial responsibility of in fact mismanaging that resource over the last years and provide financial assistance to help people and communities survive the present storm.
Last, they might undertake in consultation with the industry and representatives of the workers a full environmental impact assessment of the technology presently used in both the deep-sea and mid-shore fishery with a view to seeking an effective determination of what is necessary to ensure sustainable development.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the federal government has been providing strong and growing support to the financially weaker provinces through regional assistance.
In the case of equalization, entitlements have increased by over $3 billion in the past five years from $5.1 billion in 1985-86 to an estimated $8.2 billion in 1990-91.
These increases have occurred in every single year. In 1986-87 there was an increase of $632 million or 12.3 per cent; in 1987-88 an increase of $813 million or 14.1 per cent; in 1988-89, $661 million or 10 per cent; in 1989-90, $511 million or 7 per cent; and in 1990-91, $449 million or 5.8 per cent.
Adjournment Debate
These increases have been substantially higher than those for federal program spending as a whole and strong increases have applied to all provinces.
Prince Edward Island provides a typical example of the pattern of increases with its entitlements having increased from $134 million in 1985-86 to $203 million in 1990-91. The annual increases to this province have been $4 million, $15 million, $15 million, $15 million and $11 million for this five-year period. These are not cuts. What does happen for any given year is that successive estimates of entitlements are made and sometimes a province's entitlement for a given year will be lower than in the previous estimate for that year.
This happened for some provinces in the case of recent estimates carried out in March and covering a period of four years from 1987-88 to 1990-91.
The important thing to note is that on a year over year basis there was not a single province that had a reduction in this entitlement during the four-year period. The year over year growth rates were in almost all cases about 5 per cent and in many instances well above this level.
We would also like to refer to federal spending on regional development. This includes expenditures funded through the new regional development agencies, the regional program activities of industry, science and technology and the expenditures of other departments under federal-provincial regional development agreements. This has also increased strongly under the present government, thus average annual expenditures for these programs or their predecessors have increased from $558 million for the period from 1979-80 to 1983-84, to $832 million from 1984-85 to 1988-89 and to $1,107 billion from 1989-90 to 1994-95.
The Atlantic provinces' share of these totals increased throughout this time frame from 33 per cent for the first period to 34 per cent for the second period to an estimated 38 per cent for the last period.
These and many other examples all illustrate the high priority given by this government to the needy provinces.
